units.title: The Church as an Object of Faith: the Marks, the Primacy, the College, Reception and the Grades of Assent

lessons.title: The Church the creed names: the four marks, 'subsists in', and the limits of the claim
lessons.explanation: Lesson 76 treated the creed as a source and lesson 71 its trinitarian articles; this lesson turns to the third article, where the Church herself becomes an object of confession rather than the body that does the confessing. The creed of 381 does not say that the Church has four admirable qualities. It confesses 'one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church', which means that these are properties of the Church as God gives her to be, not the results of a survey. That difference governs everything that follows, because a mark that is confessed has to be reconciled with the empirical state of the institution, and the Church's modern documents do the reconciling by distinguishing what the Church is in herself from the sins and deficiencies of her members. The governing text is Lumen Gentium 8: 'This Church constituted and organized in the world as a society, subsists in the Catholic Church, which is governed by the successor of Peter and by the Bishops in communion with him, although many elements of sanctification and of truth are found outside of its visible structure. These elements, as gifts belonging to the Church of Christ, are forces impelling toward catholic unity.' The word 'subsists' is the crux, and the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith's responses of 29 June 2007 are the most precise gloss the magisterium has given it. They explain that the term refers to the mark of unity professed in the creed, that 'the word subsists can only be attributed to the Catholic Church alone', and at the same time that 'the Church of Christ is present and operative in the churches and ecclesial Communities not yet fully in communion with the Catholic Church, on account of the elements of sanctification and truth that are present in them'. Three levels of claim are therefore in play. Defined, and part of the Church's faith from the beginning, is the confession of one Church with the four marks, together with the necessity of the Church for salvation. Authoritative but not defined is the affirmation that the one Church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church, which is taught by a council and interpreted by a Roman congregation, and which asks for the assent proper to such teaching rather than the assent of faith. Legitimate theological opinion is the precise account of how the elements outside the visible structure relate to the one Church: whether they constitute an imperfect communion in the strict sense, how the term 'sister Churches' is to be used of patriarchates, and how the marks can be said to be present in a community that lacks full communion.
lessons.example: A catechist preparing a confirmation class asks the practical version of the question: is a local Methodist congregation part of the Church? Work the texts in order and the answer becomes a set of distinctions rather than a verdict. First, the community is not nothing: Lumen Gentium 8 says elements of sanctification and truth are found outside the Catholic Church's visible structure, and the 2007 responses say the Church of Christ is 'present and operative' in such communities, so a Catholic who describes a Methodist congregation as a purely human association has stopped reading at the first clause of the paragraph. Second, the community is not a branch: the same responses hold that 'subsists' can be predicated only of the Catholic Church, because the one Church confessed in the creed is not a federation of which the Catholic Church is a part, and the language of 'sister Churches' is reserved, in the Holy See's usage, for particular churches and patriarchates, not for the Catholic Church as a whole in relation to a Protestant community. Third, the community's standing has a technical name in Catholic usage that the catechist should learn: Unitatis Redintegratio 13 to 15 calls the Eastern bodies churches, because they retain a valid episcopate and Eucharist, while communities that grew from the sixteenth century are usually called ecclesial Communities, a usage that registers a real difference in what has been retained rather than a judgment about the sincerity of their members. Fourth, none of this settles the eternal state of any person, which Lumen Gentium 16 leaves to God's grace. The catechist who can say all four things, without softening the second or the third, has the doctrine.
lessons.question: A participant in an adult formation group says that because the Church of Christ 'subsists in' the Catholic Church, and because the Pope has called non-Catholic communities 'churches' in some speeches, the Catholic claim to be the one Church has effectively been abandoned. How should the group's leader answer?
lessons.answer: By distinguishing the claim from its application. The claim is that the one Church of Christ, with all that Christ gave her, continues in the Catholic Church governed by the successor of Peter and the bishops in communion with him; the 2007 responses state that this is what 'subsists' means and that the word cannot be predicated of another community. The application is the recognition, stated in the same paragraph of Lumen Gentium 8 and developed in Unitatis Redintegratio, that elements of sanctification and truth exist outside the visible structure and that the Spirit uses separated communities as instruments of salvation. Courtesy in speech and the use of the word 'church' for bodies with a valid episcopate do not revoke the first claim; they follow from the second. What would revoke it is a magisterial act saying that another community subsists the one Church of Christ, and no such act exists.
lessons.distractor: By agreeing that the claim has been softened: since the Second Vatican Council the Catholic Church no longer holds that she is the one Church, but that she is a particular realisation of a wider reality that includes other churches, which is why the Council replaced 'is' with 'subsists' and why the 2007 document speaks of the Church of Christ being present and operative elsewhere.
lessons.correction: The distractor reverses the direction of the change and then mistakes a qualification for a retreat. The 2007 responses were issued precisely because 'subsists' was being read as a weakening, and their answer is that the word was chosen to say something stronger and more exact than 'is': the one Church of Christ continues in the Catholic Church, and that continuity cannot be transferred to another body. The presence of the Church of Christ in separated communities, which the distractor quotes, is affirmed by the same document, but as the presence of gifts and elements, not as a second subsistence. The distractor also conflates the vocabulary of ecumenism with the vocabulary of ecclesiology: 'sister Churches', 'separated brethren' and 'ecclesial Communities' are terms with defined ranges, and using them correctly is part of obeying the doctrine rather than a way of escaping it. A group leader who teaches the distractor leaves the class unable to say why the Catholic Church does not simply merge with the others.

depth.definitions: Marks of the Church: the four properties confessed in the creed of Constantinople, one, holy, catholic and apostolic, understood as gifts of Christ to his Church rather than as empirical descriptions. Subsistence: the continued existence of the one Church of Christ in the Catholic Church, the sense the 2007 responses give the word 'subsists' in Lumen Gentium 8. Particular church: a diocese, the portion of the People of God gathered around its bishop, which is the Church in that place and not a branch of a larger company. Ecclesial Community: the term used in Catholic documents for communities of the Reformation that lack the sacramental ministry of a bishop in apostolic succession. Extra ecclesiam nulla salus: the traditional formula that there is no salvation outside the Church, taught at Florence in the decree for the Jacobites (1442) and interpreted by Lumen Gentium 14 and 16. Communion: the relation of shared faith, sacraments and ministry that admits of degrees, which is why the documents speak of imperfect communion rather than of pure exclusion. Prerequisites: the creed as a source (76), the marks in relation to the Trinity (71), and the doctrine/opinion distinction used throughout the level.
depth.mechanism: How can the same paragraph say that the one Church subsists in the Catholic Church and that elements of truth are found outside her? By distinguishing what makes the Church the Church from what she possesses. Unity in the confession of faith, the sacraments and the apostolic ministry is not a commodity distributed in portions; it is a relation to Christ, and the Church is one because her head is one. The 2007 responses put the point in terms of the creed's mark of unity: 'subsists' is predicated of the Catholic Church alone because the unity the creed professes is realised there, while the elements outside are real gifts that tend toward that unity, which is why Lumen Gentium calls them 'forces impelling toward catholic unity'. The mechanism is therefore teleological rather than quantitative. A gift outside the visible structure is not a fragment of a divided Church but a dynamism ordered to full communion, which is why the Catholic account of ecumenism is not negotiation between equals but the gathering of what already belongs to Christ into the unity he gives. Two consequences follow. The first is that the deficiencies of the separated communities, which Unitatis Redintegratio 3 mentions in the language of defects, are defects relative to the fullness, not verdicts on the faith of individuals. The second is that the Catholic Church's own deficiencies, which the same council acknowledges in the members who sin, do not touch the gifts Christ has entrusted to her, because the promise concerns the Church's constitution and not the worthiness of her ministers. A student who has this mechanism can explain why both halves of Lumen Gentium 8 belong to one doctrine.
depth.secondExample: Take the older formula and watch how a later council governs its reading. Florence's decree for the Jacobites taught that no one outside the Catholic Church, 'not only pagans but also Jews or heretics and schismatics', can share in eternal life unless joined to her before death. That is a real conciliar text and it was not withdrawn. Lumen Gentium 14 then states the formula in a way that specifies its subject: those 'who, knowing that the Catholic Church was founded as necessary by God through Christ, would refuse either to enter it or to remain in it' cannot be saved. Lumen Gentium 16 adds that those who through no fault of their own do not know the gospel or the Church, yet seek God sincerely and follow the law written on their hearts, may attain everlasting salvation. The two later texts do not deny Florence; they identify the conditions under which the necessity of the Church bears on a person's salvation, namely knowledge and refusal. This is the pattern the whole unit will use: an older formula, a later specification, and a doctrine that is one in substance and more precise in application. The transferable skill is to ask, of any hard formula, whether the later documents have specified its subject, its conditions, or its terms, and to state which of those has happened rather than announcing a reversal or pretending that nothing has been said.
depth.mistake: Two errors dominate, and they are mirror images. The first is branch theory: 'subsists in' is read as 'is one instance of', so the Catholic Church becomes a denomination among denominations and the claim to be the one Church is quietly withdrawn while the vocabulary is retained. The diagnostic is simple: branch theory cannot explain why the 2007 responses deny that 'subsists' can be predicated of any other community, and it cannot explain why Unitatis Redintegratio distinguishes churches from ecclesial Communities at all. The second error is a rigorism that reads the elements outside as mere bait, so that non-Catholic Christians are treated as though outside grace and the Church's own documents about imperfect communion and about invincible ignorance are set aside. Its diagnostic is equally simple: it has to explain away Lumen Gentium 8's second half, Lumen Gentium 16, and the 2007 responses' statement that the separated communities 'are deprived neither of significance nor importance in the mystery of salvation'. A third and subtler error is the ecumenical one: treating 'full communion' as a goal to be achieved by agreeing on a text, when the documents describe it as a gift to be received, which is why the Church's ecumenism is described as a return and a gathering rather than as a merger. All three errors share one cause, which is the failure to hold a defined confession and its authoritative application in the same act of mind.
depth.application: Task (nonblocking, 45 minutes): build a three-column sheet headed DEFINED, AUTHORITATIVE, OPINION, and place on it the following claims, each with the text that supports it: that the Church is one, holy, catholic and apostolic; that the Church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church; that the Church is necessary for salvation; that the elements of sanctification outside the visible structure impel toward catholic unity; that a particular separated community is an ecclesial Community rather than a church in the technical sense; and that 'sister Churches' may be used of the Catholic Church in relation to the Orthodox. Then write, for each item, one sentence beginning 'This does not say that...', naming what the claim leaves open. Model line: 'That the Church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church does not say that grace is absent elsewhere, since Lumen Gentium 8 affirms elements of sanctification outside the visible structure.' Rubric: every entry must carry a document and a paragraph or section; the DEFINED column must contain no more than three items; the OPINION column must include at least one position that the student does not hold. A sheet that puts everything in one column has failed, and so has a sheet that puts the necessity of the Church in the opinion column.
depth.summary: The third article of the creed makes the Church an object of faith, and the four marks are confessed rather than observed. Lumen Gentium 8 states that the one Church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church governed by Peter's successor and the bishops in communion with him, while elements of sanctification and truth are found outside her visible structure, and the 2007 responses of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith explain that 'subsists' names the continuation of the one Church and cannot be predicated of another community, even as they affirm that the Church of Christ is present and operative in communities not yet in full communion. The marks and the necessity of the Church are defined; the identification of the one Church with the Catholic Church is authoritative teaching; the theological account of how the elements outside relate to the one Church is legitimately debated. The characteristic errors are branch theory, which dissolves the claim, and rigorism, which denies the elements, and both are cured by reading the whole paragraph rather than half of it.

readings.title: Second Vatican Council, Lumen Gentium (1964), sections 7-8 and 14-16
readings.note: Read section 8 twice, slowly, and mark the two halves of the sentence about subsistence and about the elements outside. Then read 14 for the specification of the necessity of the Church, with its condition of knowledge and refusal, and 16 for those who through no fault of their own do not know the gospel. Section 7 supplies the scriptural basis in the Body of Christ, which is what makes the marks properties of a relation to Christ rather than of an institution. Holy See edition.

readings.title: Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, Responses to Some Questions Regarding Certain Aspects of the Doctrine on the Church (29 June 2007)
readings.note: This is the controlling interpretation for the lesson. Read the first two questions and answers in full: the meaning of 'subsists in', and why the expression was adopted instead of 'is'. Note the two claims held together, that the word can be attributed to the Catholic Church alone and that the Church of Christ is present and operative in other communities on account of the elements they retain. Read also the answer on the term 'sister Churches' if the page includes it, since that is the term most often misused in parish discussion.

readings.title: Second Vatican Council, Unitatis Redintegratio (1964), sections 2-4 and 13-15
readings.note: Read 2-4 for the Council's account of the elements that belong to the one Church and exist outside full communion, and 13-15 for the difference in Catholic usage between the Eastern churches and the communities of the Reformation. The section on the Eastern churches is the textual basis for saying that a body with a valid episcopate and Eucharist is called a church in a sense that a sixteenth-century community is not. Holy See edition.

readings.title: Council of Florence, decree for the Jacobites (Cantate Domino, 1442), in the decrees of the ecumenical councils
readings.note: Read the section on the necessity of the Church and on the four marks, which is the older formula that Lumen Gentium 14 and 16 later specify. This is a reproduction of a public-domain translation on a private site, not the Holy See edition, and the paragraph numbering differs from the Vatican's; use it to see the shape of the conciliar text, and quote the Catechism or Lumen Gentium when you need a citation you can defend.

lessons.title: Vatican I: what Pastor Aeternus defined, and the four conditions inside the definition
lessons.explanation: Lesson 23 set out the difference between a definition and other teaching acts, and lesson 64 described how a council works; this lesson reads the one conciliar text that makes the difference concrete. The First Vatican Council opened on 8 December 1869 with some seven hundred bishops present and produced two constitutions before it was overtaken by events: Dei Filius on faith and reason, and Pastor Aeternus on the Church, promulgated on 18 July 1870 in the fourth session. On the vote, 535 bishops were present, 533 gave their placet and two voted against; some sixty bishops of the minority had left Rome before the session rather than vote against the definition. Italian troops entered Rome on 20 September, the council was suspended on 20 October, and it never resumed or formally closed, which is why there is no conciliar decree on the episcopate and why Lumen Gentium 22 to 27 had to complete what 1870 left unfinished. The fourth chapter of Pastor Aeternus is the text that matters: 'we teach and define as a divinely revealed dogma that when the Roman pontiff speaks ex cathedra, that is, when, in the exercise of his office as shepherd and teacher of all Christians, in virtue of his supreme apostolic authority, he defines a doctrine concerning faith or morals to be held by the whole Church, he possesses, by the divine assistance promised to him in blessed Peter, that infallibility which the divine Redeemer willed his Church to enjoy in defining doctrine concerning faith or morals. Therefore, such definitions of the Roman pontiff are of themselves, and not by the consent of the Church, irreformable.' Four conditions are written into the sentence itself: the act of teaching as shepherd and teacher of all Christians, the exercise of supreme apostolic authority, a doctrine of faith or morals, and a definition proposed to the whole Church to be held. The grace promised is the Church's own infallibility, lodged personally in the pope for that act, which is why the definition says 'that infallibility which the divine Redeemer willed his Church to enjoy' rather than inventing a separate papal charism. What the council did not define is equally important: it said nothing about the episcopate's collective authority, nothing about the infallibility of the ordinary magisterium, nothing about the pope's personal holiness or his competence in politics, science or economics, and nothing that makes a definition independent of the faith once delivered. Lumen Gentium 25 later states the limit explicitly: this infallibility 'extends as far as the deposit of Revelation extends'.
lessons.example: Take five acts and run the four conditions over them, because the exercise is the lesson. Ineffabilis Deus (1854) and Munificentissimus Deus (1950) satisfy all four: each pope speaks as universal pastor, invokes supreme apostolic authority, defines a doctrine of faith, and proposes it to the whole Church to be held as divinely revealed. An apostolic letter such as Ordinatio Sacerdotalis (1994) satisfies the first three conditions but is not a definition, which is why the 1995 response of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith grounds its authority in the ordinary and universal magisterium rather than in the 1870 definition. An encyclical such as Veritatis Splendor (1993) teaches as universal pastor with supreme authority, but its argumentative paragraphs are not definitions and its authority varies within the text, which is why lesson 34 insisted on the speaker, the act, the addressee and the claim. A homily at a Wednesday audience satisfies none of the conditions in the strict sense, even when the pope is expounding doctrine, because a homily is not a definition proposed to the whole Church. A canonisation involves a definitive judgment of the Church but its object is the sanctity of a person, not a doctrine of faith or morals, which is why theologians class it separately. The classification is not a game of ranking importance: it answers the practical question of what a Catholic owes each act, and the answer differs, from the assent of faith to religious submission to attentive respect.
lessons.question: A student argues that since Pastor Aeternus says papal definitions are irreformable 'of themselves, and not by the consent of the Church', a pope could in principle define a doctrine contradicting an earlier definition or the plain sense of Scripture, and it would bind. Where exactly does the argument fail?
lessons.answer: It fails on the object and the subject of the promise. The object is a doctrine of faith or morals, which the council understands as the deposit once delivered to the saints, and Lumen Gentium 25 states that the infallibility 'extends as far as the deposit of Revelation extends, which must be religiously guarded and faithfully expounded'. A definition contradicting Scripture or an earlier definition would not be an exposition of the deposit but its denial, and the assistance promised is assistance to the Church's indefectibility in confessing what she has received, not a power of innovation. The subject is also instructive: the charism is 'that infallibility which the divine Redeemer willed his Church to enjoy', so the pope's act is the Church's act in a personal mode, which is why the definition can say the doctrine is defined 'to be held by the whole Church'. The 'of themselves' clause concerns consent, not content: it says a definition does not wait for ratification, not that it can invent its object.
lessons.distractor: It fails only in practice, because no pope has ever done it; in principle the definition is unlimited, since the council deliberately attached no condition to the object beyond 'faith or morals', and the only check on a pope is the fear of scandal, which is a political rather than a doctrinal restraint.
lessons.correction: The distractor converts a prudential observation into the whole answer and then asserts an unlimited object that the text does not give. 'Faith or morals' is not an empty formula: it names the deposit, and the same council's Dei Filius describes faith as assenting to what God has revealed, while Lumen Gentium 25 confines the charism to the deposit's extent. The distractor also confuses the two clauses of the definition. The conditions describe the act; the 'of themselves' clause describes the act's effect in relation to the Church's consent. Treating the clause as a statement about content makes the definition say something no council said, and it produces a papacy that could contradict the faith it exists to guard, which is not a strong doctrine of the office but a self-defeating one. The historical record is relevant too, though not decisive: the absence of such a definition is what one would expect if the object is the deposit, and the minority bishops who submitted after 1870 did so on exactly this reading, as the German bishops' pastoral from Fulda explained to their people in September 1870.

depth.definitions: Ex cathedra: the act described in Pastor Aeternus chapter 4, teaching as universal pastor with supreme apostolic authority in a definition of faith or morals proposed to the whole Church. Definition: a definitive act by which the Church proposes a doctrine as revealed or as definitively to be held, with the assent of faith or the firm holding that follows. Irreformable: incapable of being revised, the note Pastor Aeternus attaches to definitions 'of themselves'. Ordinary and immediate jurisdiction: the term of chapter 3, asserting that the pope's governing authority is not mediated by bishops and is not merely supervisory. Deposit of revelation: the revelation given in Christ and entrusted to the Church, which is the object and limit of infallibility. Extraordinary magisterium: the Church's teaching in a definition, whether by a council or by the pope speaking ex cathedra. Prerequisites: the acts of the teaching office (23), reading a document (34), how a council works (64), and the ecclesiology of Lumen Gentium (81).
depth.mechanism: How does a personal charism serve a corporate promise? The mechanism is representation in the strict sense: the pope acts as head of the college and as universal pastor, so his definitive act is the act of the Church in her head, not a private opinion elevated by office. Pastor Aeternus says the assistance is 'that infallibility which the divine Redeemer willed his Church to enjoy in defining doctrine', and Lumen Gentium 25 completes the picture by locating the same infallibility in the body of bishops when it teaches with Peter's successor. The two are not competing reservoirs. The college never acts without its head, the head always acts as head of the college, and the same Spirit is promised to both because the subject is one. This is why the practical effect of a definition is described in Lumen Gentium 25 as an impossibility of the Church's assent being wanting: the definition does not need to be received in order to be true, and it cannot fail to be received in the Church's faith, because the Spirit who guards the definition also guards the Church's confession. Understanding this mechanism dissolves two apparent conflicts: it shows why a definition needs no ratification without making the faithful passive, and it shows why the pope's ordinary teaching, which is not a definition, still asks for real assent of a different grade. The student who can state the mechanism in three sentences has the doctrine; the student who can state it without using the phrase 'the pope is infallible' has understood it.
depth.secondExample: Read chapter 3, not chapter 4, for the ecumenical case. Pastor Aeternus defines that the Roman pontiff possesses 'full and supreme power of jurisdiction over the whole Church, not only in matters of faith and morals, but also in those which concern the discipline and government of the Church throughout the world', and it anathematises anyone who says that this power is merely one of 'inspection or direction' or that it is not 'ordinary and immediate' over all churches, pastors and faithful. That is a distinct claim from infallibility, it was defined in the same constitution, and it is the claim that Orthodox theology has found hardest. The Second Vatican Council did not withdraw it: Lumen Gentium 22 repeats that the pope has 'full, supreme and universal power over the Church' and is always free to exercise it, while Lumen Gentium 27 teaches that bishops have in their dioceses 'all the ordinary, proper and immediate power required for the exercise of their pastoral office'. Both jurisdictions are called ordinary and immediate, and the Council's solution is not competition but sacramental grounding: the bishops' authority is not a delegation from the pope but is conferred in episcopal consecration, and the pope's authority is the principle of the unity that makes their authority ecclesial rather than local. The transferable lesson is that the famous definition of 1870 is one article in a constitution about jurisdiction, and that the ecumenical difficulty lies as much in chapter 3 as in chapter 4.
depth.mistake: The dominant popular error extends infallibility to everything the pope says or does, and it is worth naming its symptoms: quoting a papal interview as a proof text, treating an encyclical's economic argument as a matter of faith, and concluding that a change of discipline is a change of doctrine. The error's root is that it attaches the charism to the person rather than to the act, which is exactly what the four conditions exclude; its cure is to ask, of any papal text, whether it is a definition, and if not, what grade of act it is. The second error is historical: the claim that the definition of 1870 was invalid because the minority bishops had left Rome before the vote, or because the council was not formally closed. That argument confuses conciliar legitimacy with unanimity, and it is answered by the fact that the minority, including theologians who had opposed the definition, submitted afterwards and explained the definition to their churches in the terms the council had used. A third error, subtler than either, is to treat Vatican I and Vatican II as rival authorities, so that one must be preferred to the other. Lumen Gentium 18 to 25 quotes and presupposes Pastor Aeternus; the later council completes the earlier one, and a Catholic who sets them against each other has misread both.
depth.application: Task (nonblocking, 50 minutes): compile a table of six papal acts, at least two of them from the last thirty years, with columns for the four conditions of Pastor Aeternus, a column headed GRADE (definition, definitive non-definitional teaching, authentic non-definitive teaching), and a column headed WHAT IT ASKS OF ME. For each act, write one sentence beginning 'This act does not...', naming a claim it does not make. Model entry: 'An encyclical's policy recommendations do not enjoy the infallibility of a definition, because the object of the promise is a doctrine of faith or morals, not a judgment about means (Pastor Aeternus, chapter 4; Lumen Gentium 25).' Rubric: at least one entry must be a text whose grade you initially misjudged and then corrected, with a note on what misled you; the table must include one act that satisfies all four conditions; and no entry may describe the grade without a sentence saying what response it asks. A table that assigns the same grade to every act has failed the exercise, and so has one that leaves the final column empty.
depth.summary: Pastor Aeternus, promulgated on 18 July 1870, defines that when the Roman pontiff speaks ex cathedra, teaching as shepherd and teacher of all Christians, in virtue of supreme apostolic authority, defining a doctrine of faith or morals to be held by the whole Church, he enjoys that infallibility with which Christ willed his Church to be endowed, and that such definitions are irreformable of themselves and not by the consent of the Church. The four conditions are internal to the definition, the charism is the Church's own lodged personally in her head, and the object is bounded by the deposit of revelation, as Lumen Gentium 25 states. The council defined nothing about the episcopate, about the ordinary magisterium, or about the pope's competence outside faith and morals, and its chapter 3 on ordinary and immediate jurisdiction is as important for ecumenical discussion as chapter 4. The characteristic errors are extending infallibility to everything a pope says and treating the definition as an unlimited power of innovation; both are cured by reading the act rather than the office.

readings.title: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus (18 July 1870), Latin text of the four chapters and canons
readings.note: This is the Holy See's Latin editio of the constitution, and it is the text to read for the exact wording: chapter 4 contains 'docemus et divinitus revelatum dogma esse definimus' and the clause 'ex sese, non autem ex consensu Ecclesiae, irreformabiles'. The English sentences quoted in the lesson are a working translation of this Latin. Read chapter 3 as well, for the canons on ordinary and immediate jurisdiction, which are where the ecumenical difficulty actually lies.

readings.title: The First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus in English, with the historical introduction to the council
readings.note: Use this for a continuous English reading of the constitution and for the account of the sessions, the vote and the suspension of the council after the occupation of Rome. It is a reproduction of a public-domain translation on a private site, not the Holy See edition, and its bracketed numbers refer to Denzinger; check any sentence you intend to quote against the Latin at vatican.va before using it in an essay.

readings.title: Second Vatican Council, Lumen Gentium (1964), sections 18-25
readings.note: Read 18-20 for the episcopate, which Vatican I could not treat, and 25 for the two modes of infallible teaching: the pope's definitive act, and the body of bishops teaching with him. The sentence 'this infallibility extends as far as the deposit of Revelation extends' is in 25 and is the answer to the student's objection in this lesson. Note also that 25 quotes and presupposes Pastor Aeternus rather than replacing it.

readings.title: Pope John Paul II, Ut Unum Sint (1995), sections 88-96 on the ministry of the Bishop of Rome
readings.note: Read 88-96 for the only papal text in which a pope invites a fraternal re-reading of the forms in which the Petrine ministry is exercised. Note carefully what is and is not offered: the invitation concerns the exercise of the ministry, not its existence, and the section on the papacy's divine institution is not reopened. This is the correct place to see how a defined doctrine can be discussed ecumenically without being negotiated.

lessons.title: Collegiality and synodality: Lumen Gentium 22-25, the Nota Praevia, and what a synod is not
lessons.explanation: Lesson 82 ended with the gap that 1870 left: Pastor Aeternus defined the primacy and said nothing about the episcopate, because the council was suspended before it could treat the subject. Lumen Gentium 22 to 27 is the Church's answer, and it is more careful than either its admirers or its critics usually notice. The key sentence of 22 is that 'the order of bishops, which succeeds to the college of apostles and gives this apostolic body continued existence, is also the subject of supreme and full power over the universal Church, provided we understand this body together with its head the Roman Pontiff and never without this head'. The clause is not decoration. At the direction of Paul VI the Theological Commission attached an explanatory note to the constitution in November 1964, and its four points govern the reading: 'college' is not to be taken in the strictly juridical sense of a group of equals who delegate authority to their chairman; the distinction is between the pope alone and the pope with the bishops, not between the pope and the bishops taken as a rival body; the college always and of necessity includes its head, and certain acts belong to the pope alone, such as convoking and directing the college; and a collegial act in the strict sense requires the free decision of the pope, since no college can act without its head. The note also insists on something more than law: episcopal consecration confers a real participation in the apostolic office, a 'consecratory grace', while the concrete assignment of subjects and tasks is a canonical determination. Lumen Gentium 25 completes the doctrinal side by teaching that the infallibility promised to the Church is present in the body of bishops when, with Peter's successor, they exercise the supreme magisterium in a definitive act, while no individual bishop is infallible. Upon that foundation the modern synods were built. Paul VI instituted the Synod of Bishops in 1965, canon 343 of the Code of Canon Law gives it a consultative vote, and Francis's apostolic constitution Episcopalis Communio (2018) both restated that limit and refused the inference that consultation is negligible: a morally unanimous vote, it says, 'has a qualitative ecclesial weight which surpasses the merely formal aspect of the consultative vote', and article 18 provides that a Final Document expressly approved by the pope 'participates in the ordinary Magisterium of the Successor of Peter'. The October 2024 assembly tested that machinery in the most public way yet, when its Final Document was published with papal approval and no post-synodal exhortation followed.
lessons.example: Take the ordinary case and walk it through the instruments. A diocesan bishop returns from a synodal assembly and tells his people that 'the synod has decided' that a particular pastoral practice should change. Three questions sort out what has happened. First, was the assembly a council or a synod? A synod is not a council: it is a consultative body convoked by the pope, canon 343 governs its vote, and it cannot define doctrine or legislate for the universal Church. Second, did the pope expressly approve and publish the Final Document? If he did, Episcopalis Communio article 18 makes that document an act of his ordinary magisterium, which asks for religious submission under canon 752; if he did not, the document remains the assembly's advice. Third, is the practice in question discipline or doctrine? A change in the age for confirmation, the structure of parish councils or the translation of a liturgical text is discipline, and the synod may recommend it, the conference of bishops may legislate it within its competence, and the Apostolic See may approve or decline. None of that touches a defined doctrine. The bishop's sentence, 'the synod has decided', therefore compresses three quite different operations, and the compression matters because it leaves his people unable to tell a doctrinal claim from a procedural one. A better sentence would name the document, the act that approved it, and the level at which it binds.
lessons.question: A journalist writes that the Synod of Bishops has 'voted to change Church teaching' and that the pope 'must now implement the vote', while a canonist replies that since the synod's vote is only consultative, nothing it produces can bind the faithful. Which account of the synod is correct, and what does each get wrong?
lessons.answer: The canonist has the law right and the consequence wrong, and the journalist has both wrong. By canon 343 the synod has a consultative vote, so it cannot change doctrine or legislate; a vote is not a definition, and no arithmetic of votes can produce one. But Episcopalis Communio article 18 provides that a Final Document expressly approved by the Roman Pontiff participates in his ordinary magisterium, and ordinary magisterial teaching binds under canon 752 even though it is not infallible. The constitution also insists that a consultative role does not make the body negligible, since a morally unanimous vote carries a qualitative ecclesial weight beyond its formal status. So the journalist is wrong to describe a vote as a change of teaching but right that something authoritative may emerge; the canonist is right about the vote but wrong to conclude that nothing binds, because the binding act, when it occurs, is the pope's approval of the document, not the assembly's vote.
lessons.distractor: The canonist is correct on both points: a consultative body produces advice, the pope is free to ignore it, and a Catholic who treats a synod's Final Document as teaching has confused a committee with a council. Only a council in session with the pope, or the pope speaking ex cathedra, can produce teaching that binds.
lessons.correction: The distractor preserves the correct denial and adds a false one, which is the characteristic move of the over-cautious reader. It is true that a synod is not a council and cannot define; it is false that the only binding teaching acts are definitions and conciliar decrees, since the Church's ordinary magisterium binds continuously and canon 752 gives it a legislative expression. The distractor also misses the precise mechanism in Episcopalis Communio, which does not make the synod a teaching body but makes the pope's approval of its Final Document an act of his own ordinary magisterium. What the distractor fears is the inflation of every synodal document into dogma; what it produces is the opposite error, the deflation of approved teaching into advice, and both errors come from the same refusal to distinguish the grades of act. The correct answer names three things: the consultative vote, the papal act of approval, and the grade of teaching that results.

depth.definitions: Collegiality: the doctrine that the bishops, with the pope as head, form a college that is the subject of supreme and full power in the Church, taught in Lumen Gentium 22 and qualified by the Nota Praevia of 1964. Nota Praevia: the explanatory note attached at Paul VI's direction, whose four points limit the juridical sense of 'college' and reserve certain acts to the pope. Consecratory grace: the participation in the apostolic office conferred by episcopal consecration, distinguished from the canonical assignment of a diocese. Synod of Bishops: the consultative assembly instituted by Paul VI in 1965, governed by canon 343 and reorganised by Episcopalis Communio (2018). Synodality: the whole Church's mode of proceeding by consultation, discernment and reception, of which the synod is one instrument. Particular council: a plenary or provincial council with legislative authority in its territory, which is not the same thing as a synod of bishops. Prerequisites: Vatican I and its silences (82), the grades of assent (85), and the constitution of the Church (81).
depth.mechanism: The mechanism by which collegiality and primacy coexist is neither balance nor compromise but a single subject with a head. Lumen Gentium 22 does not set the college over against the pope; it defines the college as the body that cannot exist without him, and the Nota Praevia draws the consequence that the pope alone can perform certain acts, because a body without its head is not a body. Within that structure, two things are true at once and neither is a concession: the pope possesses full, supreme and universal power and is always free to exercise it, and the bishops possess in their dioceses an authority that is ordinary, proper and immediate, conferred in consecration rather than delegated (Lumen Gentium 27). The unity of the subject is what prevents the arrangement from collapsing into either absolutism or conciliarism. When the Church consults, the consultation is an exercise of that same unity: the synod gathers the sensus fidei of the faithful, the bishops discern, the pope decides whether to approve, and if he approves, the document becomes an act of his ordinary magisterium. The mechanism explains why a synod can be genuinely authoritative without being a legislature, and why a papal act of approval is not a rubber stamp on a vote but the moment at which a process becomes teaching. A student who can describe the sequence from consultation to discernment to approval to reception has understood the constitution better than most commentary on it.
depth.secondExample: Consider the case that best tests the machinery: a national bishops' conference issues a doctrinal statement on a contested public question and calls it 'the teaching of the Church in this country'. Is it? A conference is not the college. The college is the whole body of bishops with its head, and Lumen Gentium 25's promise of infallibility attaches to that body teaching definitively in union with Peter's successor, not to a regional fraction of it. Christus Dominus 4 and 8 describe the conference's competence as pastoral and legislative within its territory, and its doctrinal statements carry the weight of the bishops' authentic teaching office, which asks for religious submission under canon 752. So the statement is authoritative and not infallible, and the honest description is that it is an act of the ordinary magisterium of the bishops of that territory, approved or at least not corrected by the Apostolic See. The difference matters practically. A Catholic who rejects the statement's moral principle is in a different position from one who disputes its prudential application to a piece of legislation, and a journalist who calls either position heresy has flattened the grades. The same analysis applies to continental assemblies and to the synodal final documents before papal approval: the authority comes from the act that approves them, not from the number of participants or the warmth of the consensus.
depth.mistake: The commonest error is conciliarism in modern dress: treating any assembly of bishops as though it were the college, and therefore as though a majority could settle a doctrinal question. Its diagnostic is that it cannot say why Lumen Gentium 22 insists on 'never without this head', and it usually appeals to the early councils while ignoring that those councils were received because they taught the faith, not because they were large. The second error is the mirror image: a papal maximalism that treats every exercise of the primacy as though it made consultation superfluous, and that reads the Nota Praevia as a restriction on the council rather than an explanation of its text. Its diagnostic is that it cannot explain why the same council that defined the primacy also instituted synods, reformed the curia and asked the bishops of the world for counsel. The third error is procedural: confusing the consultative vote with an opinion poll, and hence treating a synodal document as a weather report. Episcopalis Communio's phrase about the 'qualitative ecclesial weight' of a morally unanimous vote was written against exactly that reading, and article 18's provision about the Final Document shows what the Church thinks a synod can produce. All three errors share one root, which is the refusal to hold head and body in a single act of thought.
depth.application: Task (nonblocking, 40 minutes): take the text of any synodal or conference document available to you and produce a one-page authority sheet with four lines. Line one, WHO ACTED: name the body, its competence and the instrument it used. Line two, WHAT GRADE: is this a definition, definitive teaching, authentic non-definitive teaching, or advice, and on what text do you base the classification? Line three, WHAT IT ASKS: state the response owed, with the canon or conciliar paragraph. Line four, WHAT IT DOES NOT SAY: name one thing a reader might infer that the document does not claim. Model line: 'The Final Document of the 2024 assembly, approved and published by the pope, participates in his ordinary magisterium (Episcopalis Communio, article 18, section 1), and therefore asks for religious submission of intellect and will (canon 752); it does not define doctrine, and its pastoral proposals remain subject to the bishop's implementation.' Rubric: line two must quote the text that authorises the grade, not merely assert it; line four must identify a misreading you have actually seen. A sheet whose line two reads 'important document' has not begun.
depth.summary: Lumen Gentium 22 teaches that the college of bishops with its head, and never without its head, is the subject of supreme and full power in the Church, and the Nota Praevia of 1964 fixes the sense: no college of equals, no rivalry with the primacy, no collegial act without the pope's free decision. Lumen Gentium 25 adds that the Church's infallibility is present in the body of bishops teaching definitively with Peter's successor, while no single bishop is infallible. Canon 343 gives the Synod of Bishops a consultative vote, and Episcopalis Communio (2018) holds both that consultation is weighty and that a Final Document expressly approved by the pope participates in his ordinary magisterium. The characteristic errors are treating an assembly as a legislature, treating the primacy as making counsel superfluous, and treating an approved document as advice; each is cured by naming the act, the grade and the response it asks.

readings.title: Second Vatican Council, Lumen Gentium (1964), sections 22-27, with the Nota Praevia printed with the constitution
readings.note: Read 22 three times and note the clause 'and never without this head'. Then read the Nota Praevia, which the Holy See prints with the constitution, for its four points: the non-juridical sense of 'college', the distinction between the pope alone and the pope with the bishops, the acts reserved to the pope, and the requirement of his free decision for a collegial act. Read 25 for the two modes of infallible teaching, and 27 for the bishops' ordinary, proper and immediate power in their dioceses, which is the sentence that answers the objection that collegiality and primacy must compete.

readings.title: Pope Francis, Episcopalis Communio (2018), especially articles 1-6 and 18
readings.note: Article 18 is the operative provision for this lesson: the Final Document, if expressly approved by the pope, participates in the ordinary magisterium, and section 2 provides for the case in which deliberative power has been granted under canon 343. Read the earlier articles for the three phases of consultation, discernment and decision, and for the sentence that a morally unanimous vote has a qualitative ecclesial weight surpassing the formal consultative vote. Holy See edition.

readings.title: Second Vatican Council, Christus Dominus (1965), sections 2-6 and 8 on the bishop's office and on conferences
readings.note: Read 2-6 for the theology of episcopal office, which grounds the claim that a bishop's authority is conferred in consecration rather than delegated, and 8 for what a conference of bishops may and may not do in its territory. This is the text to have in hand when someone claims that a national conference can teach definitively.

lessons.title: Reception: three senses, and why the Church's acceptance does not make a teaching true
lessons.explanation: Lesson 32 treated the tests of doctrinal development and lesson 83 the machinery of councils and synods; this lesson takes the concept that is most often invoked when a Catholic wants to argue that a teaching has or has not taken hold, and separates its senses. 'Reception' is used in three different ways in the Church's life, and nearly every confused argument about it trades on the ambiguity. The first sense is juridical: a council's or a pope's act is received into the legal order of a particular church or of a group of churches. The Eastern Catholic Churches, for instance, received the Second Vatican Council's teaching through the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches promulgated in 1990, which is reception as legislation. The second sense is theological: the whole People of God assimilates a teaching in faith, and here the controlling texts are Lumen Gentium 12, which teaches that the whole body of the faithful, anointed by the Holy One, cannot err in matters of belief, and Lumen Gentium 25, which says that to the Church's definitions 'the assent of the Church can never be wanting, on account of the activity of that same Holy Spirit'. The third sense is historical and sociological: the actual uptake of a teaching or a reform in a place and a generation, which can be slow, partial or absent. The three senses are not rival theories; they are three questions. What went wrong in most modern disputes is that one sense has been made to do the work of another, usually the third doing the work of the second. The texts that govern the theological sense are unambiguous about direction. Pastor Aeternus defines that papal definitions are irreformable 'of themselves, and not by the consent of the church', and Lumen Gentium 25 treats the Church's assent as an effect promised by the Spirit rather than a condition to be satisfied. It follows that reception cannot be a tribunal that ratifies or annuls doctrine. What it can be, and is, is an event in the Church's history whose failures are informative: they send the Church back to ask whether a formulation was defective, whether a reform was badly explained, whether a discipline was unworkable, or whether the refusal was simply sin. Benedict XVI's address to the Roman Curia of 22 December 2005 supplies the framework the Church now uses for the interpretation of a council's texts, the hermeneutic of reform in continuity, and it is a framework for reading, not for voting.
lessons.example: Florence is the cleanest historical case. In July 1439 the council promulgated the decree of union with the Greeks, which stated the Latin doctrine on the procession of the Spirit and the legitimacy of the addition to the creed, on purgatory, on the life of the blessed and on suffrages for the dead, and on the plenitude of power of the Apostolic See. The Greek delegates signed; the emperor needed military help; the union was proclaimed in Hagia Sophia in December 1439. It then collapsed. The Byzantine churches repudiated it, a synod in Constantinople in 1484 formally rejected it, and the memory of Florence became, in Orthodox polemic, the paradigm of a union imposed by pressure. Now classify. Juridically, the decree was received in the Latin Church and never revoked. Theologically, its doctrinal content was proposed by a council in union with the pope, and Lumen Gentium 25's principle applies: the assent of the Church cannot be wanting to what the Church definitively teaches. Historically, reception failed, and the failure was not irrational: the Greek delegation acted without the settled mind of their churches, the political motive was transparent, and the doctrinal formulas were Latin in idiom and were not explained in the terms the East used. The failure therefore tells you something about the circumstances, the formulation and the politics. It does not tell you that the doctrine was not taught, and it cannot be used to reopen purgatory as an open question, which is the move the lesson on 81 warned against.
lessons.question: A theologian argues in an article that because the great majority of Catholics do not accept the Church's teaching on the transmission of human life, that teaching has not been received and is therefore not binding; a correspondent replies that reception is a modernist invention and that the Church has never spoken of it. Assess both claims.
lessons.answer: Both are wrong, and the first is wrong in a way that the second cannot cure. Reception is not an invention: Lumen Gentium 12 speaks of the sensus fidei of the whole people, Lumen Gentium 25 of the Church's assent to definitions, and the Church's law and ecumenical documents use the concept constantly, so a Catholic who denies that reception exists is denying what the Council taught. But the theologian's inference fails at two points. First, non-acceptance is not the same as non-reception in the theological sense: the theological sense names the Spirit's work of assimilation, and the empirical fact that many Catholics dissent, or are badly catechised, or have never heard the teaching, is evidence about catechesis and about the state of the Church's life, not evidence that the Spirit has withheld his guidance. Second, the sensus fidei cannot be measured by a poll: Lumen Gentium 12 describes the whole people's supernatural appreciation of the faith, and it is not the majority opinion of the moment, which is why the same paragraph is always read with the teaching office that judges authentic expressions of it. The teaching set out in Humanae Vitae 14 is authoritative and not defined; its pastoral reception has been genuinely difficult; neither fact converts it into opinion.
lessons.distractor: The theologian is right in substance and the correspondent is right in principle: a moral teaching that the faithful in conscience do not receive has lost its binding force, because the Church's authority is exercised within the communion of the faithful and cannot subsist against their settled sense of the faith, which is why the Church's teaching on this question is now treated as open by most bishops.
lessons.correction: The distractor joins two errors and calls the result a synthesis. It makes the settled sense of the faithful into a tribunal over the magisterium, which inverts Lumen Gentium 25's order: the assent of the Church is promised to definitions and cannot be wanting, so a state of affairs in which assent appears to be lacking is a summons to examine the catechesis and the formulation, not a verdict on the truth. It also asserts a factual claim that is not true as stated, namely that most bishops treat the teaching as open; what exists is pastoral difficulty, disagreement among theologians about how to present the teaching, and a long argument about the weight of the encyclical, none of which amounts to a withdrawal. And it repeats the correspondent's error in a subtler form by treating reception as a single mechanism with a single effect, when the lesson's three senses have to be separated before any conclusion can be drawn. A reader who can say which sense is in play in the theologian's argument has the whole lesson.

depth.definitions: Reception, juridical: the incorporation of a teaching or a reform into the legal order of a church, as the Eastern Catholic Churches received Vatican II through the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (1990). Reception, theological: the whole People of God's assimilation of a teaching in faith, described in Lumen Gentium 12 and 25. Reception, historical: the actual uptake of a teaching or reform, which may be delayed or refused. Sensus fidei: the supernatural appreciation of the faith given to the whole body of the faithful, which cannot err in matters of belief (Lumen Gentium 12). Hermeneutic of reform: Benedict XVI's term, in the address of 22 December 2005, for reading a council's texts as reform in continuity rather than as rupture. Defect of formulation: the possibility, acknowledged in the Church's own discussions, that a true doctrine may have been stated in terms that obscured it for its hearers. Prerequisites: the tests of development (32), the acts and grades of teaching (23, 85), and conciliar machinery (64, 83).
depth.mechanism: Why is reception not a condition of truth, and why does it still matter? Because the Church's indefectibility is a promise about her faith, not about her sociology. The Spirit is promised to the Church so that she will not fail to confess what she has received, and that promise is realised in the assent of the faithful to definitions, which is what Lumen Gentium 25 asserts. Reception in the theological sense is therefore the effect of the promise, and the historical sense is the empirical trace of that effect in a particular place, which can be distorted by ignorance, scandal, politics or sin. The mechanism is thus asymmetric. A definition's truth does not wait on acceptance, but the Church's life can fail to display the acceptance, and when that happens the failure is diagnostic: it points to a defect in catechesis, in translation, in the manner of imposition, or in the formulation itself. That is why the Church's practice has been to reformulate rather than to repeat: the seventeenth-century Chinese rites dispute, the nineteenth-century debates about the Latin in the missions, and the twentieth-century liturgical translations are all cases in which the question was not whether the doctrine was true but whether the form in which it was proposed could be received. The mechanism therefore gives a student two questions instead of one: is this teaching true and authoritative, and is this formulation receivable? Confusing the two produces either a magisterium that can be outvoted or a pastoral practice that ignores the failure of its own communication.
depth.secondExample: Take the reception of Nicaea, which no one doubts, and watch how long the process took. The council of 325 defined that the Son is homoousios with the Father, and the formula was contested for more than half a century: Athanasius was exiled five times, councils in the 350s produced alternative formulas, and for a period the imperial court favoured a homoean account that avoided the disputed word altogether. The doctrine was not uncertain in the meantime; the Church's faith was being defended by a minority and eventually prevailed at Constantinople in 381, whose creed became the baptismal and liturgical norm of the whole Church. Two lessons follow. The first is that a slow or contested reception does not indicate an unsettled doctrine, since the period of the greatest confusion enclosed the most exact definition the Church has ever produced. The second is that reception is a process with stages: definition, defence, conciliar restatement, liturgical embedding, and catechesis, and the last two are what make a formula live in the Church's actual speech. A student who applies this to the modern cases will ask not 'has this been received?' but 'at which stage is it, and what is missing?' That question is answerable, whereas the first is usually a way of smuggling a verdict into a description.
depth.mistake: The progressive error makes reception into a referendum and then reads the result as a doctrinal verdict: a teaching that is widely refused has, on this account, been shown to be false or at least to have lost its force. Its diagnostic is that it must treat Lumen Gentium 25 and Pastor Aeternus as rhetorical flourishes, and it usually appeals to the sense of the faithful while ignoring that the same Council located the authentic judgment of the faith in the teaching office. The traditionalist error denies that reception is a theological category at all and treats every failure of uptake as simple disobedience, which is often true and sometimes not: the Chinese rites controversy and the history of liturgical translation show cases in which the Church itself later judged that a formulation or a policy had obstructed the faith it meant to serve. The third error is the scholarly one, which uses reception as a neutral historical description and then quietly draws doctrinal conclusions from it, so that a failure of reception becomes evidence of a defect in the doctrine rather than in its communication. All three errors can be diagnosed by a single question: is the claim being made about the truth of the teaching, about the adequacy of its formulation, or about the facts of its uptake? Only the second and third are questions reception can answer.
depth.application: Task (nonblocking, 45 minutes): choose one twentieth-century act whose reception is documented, such as the 1967 reform of indulgences, the 1969 Missal, or the 1968 encyclical on the transmission of life. Produce a three-column sheet headed JURIDICAL, THEOLOGICAL, HISTORICAL. In the juridical column, state what was promulgated, by what act and with what legal effect, citing the document. In the theological column, state what grade of teaching is involved and what response it asks, citing Lumen Gentium 25 or canon 752. In the historical column, record two pieces of evidence about uptake, one showing acceptance and one showing resistance, each with a date and a source, and then write three sentences saying what the evidence does and does not show. Model line for the last part: 'Resistance in this diocese shows that the reform was badly explained to clergy who had been trained in the older practice; it does not bear on the doctrinal question, which was settled by the Apostolic See's act of promulgation.' Rubric: the historical column must contain at least one item that complicates your own conclusion, and the final sentences must not use the word 'therefore' to move from historical evidence to doctrinal judgment.
depth.summary: Reception has three senses: the juridical incorporation of an act into a church's law, the theological assimilation of a teaching in faith, and the historical fact of its uptake. The theological sense is governed by Lumen Gentium 12 and 25 and by Pastor Aeternus: the assent of the Church cannot be wanting to definitions, and definitions are irreformable of themselves and not by the consent of the Church, so reception is an effect of the Spirit's promise rather than a condition of truth. The historical sense is real and its failures are informative, as Florence in 1439 and the long contest over Nicaea both show, but a failure of reception points to a question about formulation, communication or obedience, not to a verdict on doctrine. The characteristic error is to let the third sense do the work of the second, which turns the Church's life into a referendum; the cure is to ask, before drawing any conclusion, which of the three questions is being answered.

readings.title: Second Vatican Council, Lumen Gentium (1964), sections 12 and 25
readings.note: Read 12 for the sensus fidei: the whole body of the faithful, anointed by the Holy One, cannot err in matters of belief, and the discernment of authentic expressions of that sense belongs to the teaching office. Read 25 for the sentence that carries the lesson, that to the Church's definitions 'the assent of the Church can never be wanting', and note that it is stated as an effect of the Spirit's activity. The two paragraphs together are the reason reception cannot be a tribunal.

readings.title: Pope Benedict XVI, Address to the Roman Curia (22 December 2005), on the hermeneutic of reform
readings.note: Read the central section on the two hermeneutics, of discontinuity and rupture, and of reform in continuity, and note that the Pope applies it to the reception of the Council's texts rather than to their authority. This is the framework the modern magisterium uses for the question this lesson raises, and it shows that the Church's answer to a contested reception is interpretation rather than a recount.

readings.title: Council of Florence, decree of union with the Greeks (Laetentur Caeli, 6 July 1439)
readings.note: Read the decree and the surrounding narrative for the doctrinal content, the signing by the Greek delegates, and the political circumstances. This is a reproduction of a public-domain translation on a private site, not the Holy See edition; use it for the shape of the text and the historical sequence, and cite the decree by its date and title rather than by this page's paragraph numbers. The point of reading it is to see a doctrinal act whose historical reception failed.

readings.title: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus (1870), chapter 4, Latin text
readings.note: Read the single clause 'ex sese, non autem ex consensu Ecclesiae, irreformabiles' in its sentence. It is the textual basis for the lesson's central claim that reception does not confer authority. The English rendering used in the lesson is a working translation of this Latin; if you need to quote it in an essay, quote the Latin clause and give your own translation, or cite Lumen Gentium 25 in English.
