lessons.title: Ad Tuendam Fidem: three paragraphs, and a teaching whose grade is argued
lessons.explanation: Lesson 82 showed that infallibility attaches to a kind of act, and lesson 31 distinguished dogma from definitive teaching from authoritative teaching; this lesson reads the document that turned those distinctions into law. On 18 May 1998 John Paul II issued the motu proprio Ad Tuendam Fidem, which added a second paragraph to canon 750 of the Code of Canon Law and a parallel provision to canon 598 of the Eastern code, and attached a penalty in canon 1371 for the obstinate rejection of what is definitively to be held. The occasion was the Profession of Faith promulgated in 1989, whose three paragraphs had begun to be read as though the middle one were redundant. The first paragraph is the creed itself, professed as divinely revealed. The second reads: 'I also firmly accept and hold each and everything definitively proposed by the Church regarding teaching on faith and morals.' The third reads: 'Moreover I adhere with submission of will and intellect to the teachings which either the Roman Pontiff or the College of Bishops enunciate when they exercise their authentic Magisterium, even if they do not intend to proclaim these teachings by a definitive act.' Ad Tuendam Fidem's own explanation of the second paragraph is the crucial text: it concerns 'truths that are necessarily connected to divine revelation', truths which 'illustrate the Divine Spirit's particular inspiration for the Church's deeper understanding of a truth concerning faith and morals, with which they are connected either for historical reasons or by a logical relationship'. Two consequences follow. The second paragraph is not a softer version of the first: what is definitively proposed must be firmly held, and its rejection sets a person against the teaching of the Church. Nor is it a synonym for the first: these truths are not themselves divinely revealed, but they are required for the holy keeping and faithful exposition of what is. The third paragraph is the home of authentic but non-definitive teaching, and canon 752 gives its response, a religious submission of intellect and will rather than the assent of faith. Into this architecture the hard case falls. Ordinatio Sacerdotalis (1994) declared that 'the Church has no authority whatsoever to confer priestly ordination on women and that this judgment is to be definitively held by all the Church's faithful'. The response of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith of 28 October 1995 added that the teaching 'has been set forth infallibly by the ordinary and universal Magisterium' and is 'to be understood as belonging to the deposit of the faith'. That combination is what makes the case instructive: the act is not a definition, so the first paragraph of the Profession is not its obvious home; the response speaks of the deposit, which points to the first paragraph; and the standard commentary on Ad Tuendam Fidem, published with the motu proprio, lists the reservation of ordination among the truths of the second paragraph. The obligation is settled; the note is argued.
lessons.example: Take a case where the classification is uncontroversial, so that the machinery can be seen working before the hard case is attempted: the canonisation of a saint. When the Church canonises, she makes a definitive judgment that the person is in glory and is to be honoured as a saint, and the common theological position, argued at length by Benedict XIV in the eighteenth century, is that this judgment cannot be erroneous. But the proposition 'this man is a saint' is not a truth contained in revelation; it is a fact about a creature, known to God and infallibly certified by the Church. It therefore belongs to the second paragraph rather than the first: definitively proposed, firmly to be held, and connected to revelation by the logic of the communion of saints and by the Church's authority to bind and loose. The example does two things for the student. It shows that the second paragraph is not a device for inflating papal claims, since canonisation is a case where everyone agrees the truth is not revealed and yet the judgment is irreversible. And it shows what 'definitively proposed' adds to 'authentically taught': a Catholic may discuss the historical evidence about a candidate's virtues, and a postulator does exactly that, but once the Church has pronounced, the question is closed, and the closing is an exercise of the same assistance that guards the Church's faith.
lessons.question: A student preparing for ordination writes that Ordinatio Sacerdotalis cannot be infallible because the pope did not speak ex cathedra, and that in any case the question whether the teaching belongs to the first or the second paragraph of the Profession of Faith is one on which the Church has said nothing, so a Catholic is free to hold either view or neither. What is right and what is wrong in this?
lessons.answer: The first claim is wrong and the second is half right. Wrong: a definition is not the only mode of infallible teaching. Lumen Gentium 25 attributes infallibility to the body of bishops teaching definitively with Peter's successor, and the 1995 response expressly grounds the teaching in that ordinary and universal magisterium, adding that it is to be understood as belonging to the deposit of the faith. The absence of an ex cathedra act therefore does not leave the teaching non-definitive. Half right: the precise classification between the first and second paragraphs is genuinely argued. The 1995 response's language about the deposit points toward the first; the commentary published with Ad Tuendam Fidem lists the reservation of ordination among the second paragraph's truths; and theologians have written on both sides, some questioning whether the historical record shows a definitively taught tradition. What does not follow is the student's conclusion. Ad Tuendam Fidem binds what is definitively proposed whether it belongs to the first paragraph or the second, and canon 750 section 2 with canon 1371 attaches a penalty to obstinate rejection, so neither classification leaves the teaching open.
lessons.distractor: The first claim is right, because infallibility is a property of definitions and the 1995 response is a congregational note rather than an act of the pope teaching ex cathedra. The second is right as well, and it follows that since the classification is undetermined the teaching is at most authentic non-definitive teaching, so a Catholic may publicly argue for a change in the discipline while remaining obedient to the Church's practice.
lessons.correction: The distractor gets its force from a real feature of the case, the absence of a definition, and then misuses it twice. It treats a congregational response as though the congregation were speaking on its own authority, when the 1995 response was published with papal approval and its whole purpose was to state the grade of a teaching the pope had already proposed; a response of that kind is an act of the magisterium, not a private memorandum. It then treats the undetermined classification as though it settled the obligation, which inverts Ad Tuendam Fidem's structure: the motu proprio exists precisely because there are truths that are definitively to be held without being divinely revealed, so the second paragraph is not a way station to the third but a distinct and binding grade. The distractor also slides from the classification of the teaching to the practical conclusion about public argument, which does not follow on either classification, since even third-paragraph teaching asks for religious submission under canon 752. What remains legitimately open is the theological argument about the note; what is not open is the treatment of the teaching as one opinion among others.

depth.definitions: Dogma: a truth divinely revealed and defined, to be believed with divine and catholic faith, the first paragraph of the Profession. Definitive teaching: a truth definitively proposed by the Church as required for the faithful exposition of the deposit, firmly to be held, the second paragraph, with canon 750 section 2 as its legal expression. Authentic non-definitive teaching: teaching of the ordinary magisterium that is not proposed definitively, owed religious submission of intellect and will under canon 752, the third paragraph. Theological note: the technical classification of a teaching's weight, which is what the hard case argues about. Ordinary and universal magisterium: the body of bishops with Peter's successor teaching definitively while dispersed, the mode invoked by the 1995 response. Obstinate rejection: the canonical description of refusal after warning, penalised in canon 1371 as amended. Prerequisites: grades of assent (23, 31), the 1870 definition (82), and the ecclesiology of the college (83).
depth.mechanism: Why does the Church need a middle grade at all? Because revelation is not a list of propositions but a Person and a mystery, and the Church's understanding of it generates judgments that are neither the mystery itself nor mere policy. Ad Tuendam Fidem describes the connection in two ways: historical and logical. Historical connection: a truth may be required because of the way the Church's teaching developed, for instance a judgment about the validity of a formula that the Church's sacramental practice presupposes. Logical connection: a truth may be entailed by a revealed truth, as the illicitness of euthanasia follows from the revealed gift of life and the prohibition of murder. Neither kind is itself revealed, and both are necessary if the revealed truth is to be guarded and expounded, which is why the Church proposes them definitively and why their rejection is not a difference of theological opinion but a contradiction of the Church's teaching. The mechanism also explains the penalty. Canon 1371 as amended does not punish error as such; it punishes obstinate rejection after warning, which is a juridical description of a person setting himself against the Church's definitive proposal. A student who understands this can explain why the Church has three grades rather than two: two would force every entailment either into the creed or into opinion, and the first would inflate the creed while the second would leave the faith undefended at exactly the points where its implications are contested.
depth.secondExample: Take the second example the 1998 commentary itself offers, the illicitness of euthanasia, because it shows the middle grade doing necessary work. Evangelium Vitae 65 states that euthanasia is 'a grave violation of the law of God' and that those who cooperate in it are in a state of grave sin, and the encyclical's argument rests on the revealed truth that human life is a gift of God and on the prohibition of killing the innocent. Now ask what grade the prohibition carries. It is not a new revelation; the Fifth Commandment and the Church's constant teaching supply the premise. It is not a policy judgment, since no change in medical technology or social expectation could make it permissible. The judgment that euthanasia is always and everywhere wrong is therefore a truth definitively proposed as required for the faithful exposition of the deposit, which is exactly the second paragraph's description. The same analysis applies to the condemnation of torture, to the intrinsic character of racial discrimination, and to the impossibility of a valid marriage that excludes its essential properties. The transferable instrument is a question about dependence: does this teaching stand because a revealed truth entails it, because the Church's sacramental or doctrinal practice presupposes it, or because the Church has judged it prudent for a time? The first two place it in the second paragraph, the third in the third, and getting the question right is most of the work.
depth.mistake: One error says that only divinely revealed truths can be infallibly taught, so any teaching whose content is not in Scripture and the creed is at most opinion. Its diagnostic is that it cannot account for canonisation, for the Church's judgments about the validity of sacramental formulas, or for the condemnations of acts that the framework of Veritatis Splendor 80 treats as excluded by their object; and it reduces the second paragraph of the Profession to decoration. The opposite error says that every authoritative teaching is effectively definitive, so that a pope's allocation or a congregation's instruction leaves no room for argument. Its diagnostic is that it cannot explain why Ad Tuendam Fidem distinguishes a third paragraph at all, and it makes the theological examination of arguments impossible, which the Church's own tradition of theology requires. A third error is peculiar to the hard case: quoting the 1995 response's phrase about the deposit and the commentary's placement of the teaching in the second paragraph as though one of them must be wrong, when the more accurate description is that the reconciliation of the two is an unfinished theological task, on which serious Catholics have written on both sides without treating the teaching itself as optional. The discipline is to keep three questions apart: what is taught, what grade it carries, and what response it asks.
depth.application: Task (nonblocking, 45 minutes): take five propositions, at least three drawn from documents you have read in this level, and fill a four-column table: PROPOSITION, GRADE (first, second or third paragraph of the Profession), THE TEXT THAT SETTLES IT, and WHAT REJECTION WOULD MEAN. For every row in the second and third columns, quote the phrase that carries the grade, whether 'divinely revealed', 'definitively proposed', or 'authentic magisterium... not definitive'. Model row: 'That the eucharistic sacrifice is propitiatory for the living and the dead; first paragraph, because the Council of Trent defines it as divinely revealed in Session 22; rejection would be heresy and would also make the Church's liturgical practice unintelligible.' Rubric: at least one row must be a teaching whose grade you cannot settle from the texts alone, and that row must state what further evidence would settle it; the fourth column must distinguish heresy, refusal of definitive teaching, and refusal of religious submission. A table with two grades only has collapsed the architecture the motu proprio built.
depth.summary: Ad Tuendam Fidem (1998) added to canon 750 a second paragraph covering truths 'definitively proposed' by the Church, which are connected to revelation historically or logically, must be firmly held, and are protected by a penalty in canon 1371 for obstinate rejection; canon 752 governs the third grade, authentic non-definitive teaching, which asks for religious submission rather than the assent of faith. The three paragraphs of the Profession of Faith are therefore three grades of act with three grades of response, and the middle one exists because revelation generates entailments that are neither the creed itself nor policy. Ordinatio Sacerdotalis is the hard case: not an ex cathedra definition, yet grounded by the 1995 response in the ordinary and universal magisterium and described as belonging to the deposit, while the commentary on the motu proprio places it in the second paragraph; the obligation to hold it is settled, and the precise note is a matter of theological argument. The characteristic errors are confining infallibility to definitions and inflating every authoritative act into a definition.

readings.title: Pope John Paul II, Ad Tuendam Fidem (18 May 1998), with the amended canons
readings.note: Read the whole document, which is short, and then read the three paragraphs of the Profession of Faith that it reproduces. The sentence to mark is the one about truths 'necessarily connected to divine revelation', with its two kinds of connection, historical and logical; that sentence is the reason the middle grade exists. Note also the amendment to canon 750 and the penalty provision, since the lesson's argument depends on the obligation having a legal expression.

readings.title: Pope John Paul II, Ordinatio Sacerdotalis (22 May 1994)
readings.note: Read the final section for the two clauses the lesson quotes: that the Church has no authority to confer priestly ordination on women, and that this judgment is to be definitively held by all the faithful. Note what the document does not do: it is an apostolic letter, it does not use the form of a definition, and it does not state the theological note. That absence is what the 1995 response supplies and what makes the case a study in classification rather than in authority.

readings.title: Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, response of 28 October 1995 on Ordinatio Sacerdotalis, with the accompanying commentary
readings.note: Read the brief response and then the commentary, which explains why the congregation answered as it did. The phrases to mark are 'set forth infallibly by the ordinary and universal Magisterium' and 'belonging to the deposit of the faith', because the tension between them and the second paragraph of the Profession is the substance of the lesson's hard case. Holy See edition; the commentary is published with the response.

steps: Top rung labelled FIRST PARAGRAPH: object 'truths divinely revealed', example the eucharistic sacrifice defined at Trent Session 22, response 'assent of faith', legal expression canon 750 section 1. Annotated: rejection is heresy.

questions.prompt: In a parish discussion of Lumen Gentium 8, one participant says that because the Church of Christ 'subsists in' the Catholic Church, the Catholic Church is simply one branch among several, and another says that because the same paragraph mentions 'elements of sanctification and of truth' outside her visible structure, nothing at all is being claimed for the Catholic Church. Using Lumen Gentium 8 and the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith's 2007 responses, state what the sentence claims and what it does not.
questions.answer: The sentence claims identity, not branch membership. Lumen Gentium 8 says that 'this Church constituted and organized in the world as a society, subsists in the Catholic Church, which is governed by the successor of Peter and by the Bishops in communion with him, although many elements of sanctification and of truth are found outside of its visible structure'. The 2007 responses explain that 'subsists' was chosen precisely because it refers to the mark of unity professed in the creed, and that the word 'can only be attributed to the Catholic Church alone'. The same document concedes that the Church of Christ 'is present and operative' in communities not yet in full communion, on account of those elements, and that they 'are deprived neither of significance nor importance in the mystery of salvation'. So the paragraph asserts two things at once: the one Church of Christ continues in the Catholic Church with the fullness of the means of salvation, and real ecclesial gifts exist outside her visible bounds, which is why the separated communities are not nothing.
questions.distractor: The sentence is a diplomatic compromise that leaves the question open: 'subsists in' was chosen to avoid saying 'is', so a Catholic is free to hold either that the Catholic Church is the one Church or that she is one realisation of a wider reality, and the 2007 responses merely record the more generous of the two readings without settling anything.
questions.correction: The distractor turns a technical choice of words into an open question, which is exactly the move the 2007 document was written to block. Its whole argument is that 'subsists' is a stronger and more precise word than 'is', not a weaker one: it says that the one Church of Christ continues to exist in the Catholic Church with all that Christ gave her, and that this predicate cannot be transferred to another community. Where the distractor is right is only in noticing that the sentence is not a denial of grace outside the visible bounds; but that concession is made in the second half of the same sentence in Lumen Gentium 8, which the document quotes. A learner who holds both halves together, the identity of the one Church with the Catholic Church and the real presence of ecclesial elements elsewhere, has the doctrine; a learner who keeps one half and drops the other has either branch theory or a rigorism that Vatican II did not teach.

questions.prompt: A diocesan newspaper describes a papal homily at a Wednesday audience as 'an infallible pronouncement', and a blogger replies that papal infallibility covers everything the pope says about faith, morals, politics and economics because Pastor Aeternus says his definitions are irreformable 'of themselves'. Using the text of the 1870 definition, identify the conditions it attaches and say whether either writer has read it correctly.
questions.answer: Neither has. Pastor Aeternus, chapter 4, defines that when the Roman Pontiff speaks ex cathedra, 'that is, when, in the exercise of his office as shepherd and teacher of all Christians, in virtue of his supreme apostolic authority, he defines a doctrine concerning faith or morals to be held by the whole Church', he enjoys by divine assistance the infallibility with which Christ willed his Church to be endowed in defining doctrine, 'and therefore such definitions of the Roman pontiff are of themselves, and not by the consent of the church, irreformable'. Four conditions are therefore built into the definition: the act of teaching as universal pastor, the exercise of supreme apostolic authority, a doctrine of faith or morals, and a definition to be held by the whole Church. A homily at an audience meets none of them; economics meets the third only by an equivocation. The 'of themselves' clause answers a different question, whether a definition needs the Church's subsequent consent to be binding. It says it does not.
questions.distractor: The homily is indeed infallible, because a pope teaching on faith and morals is always protected from error, and the 'of themselves' clause means that whatever a pope defines binds immediately without any reception; the blogger is wrong only in extending the same guarantee to economics, which is not a matter of faith or morals.
questions.correction: The distractor keeps the shape of the doctrine and removes its limits, which is how the dogma is most often misstated. Infallibility is attached to a specific act, the definitive definition of a doctrine of faith or morals by the universal pastor, not to the pope's person or to his general teaching office; the Second Vatican Council states the same thing when it says that the Roman Pontiff enjoys this infallibility 'when, as the supreme shepherd and teacher of all the faithful, by a definitive act he proclaims a doctrine of faith or morals' (Lumen Gentium 25). The distractor also gets the 'of themselves' clause backwards in spirit: the clause explains why a definition does not wait for consent, and Lumen Gentium 25 adds that 'to these definitions the assent of the Church can never be wanting', which describes a promised effect, not a permission. The blogger's error is different in kind: he treats a condition about the object of the act as though it were a licence about competence.

questions.prompt: After a Synod of Bishops issues its final document, a journalist writes that 'the synod has voted to change Church teaching and the pope must now implement it', while a canonist replies that the synod's vote was only consultative and therefore carries no weight at all. Using Episcopalis Communio and canon 343, adjudicate between them.
questions.answer: Both formulations are wrong in opposite directions. Canon 343 gives the Synod of Bishops a consultative vote, and Episcopalis Communio restates the point while refusing the inference the canonist draws: the fact that the synod 'ordinarily has only a consultative role does not diminish its importance', and a morally unanimous vote 'has a qualitative ecclesial weight which surpasses the merely formal aspect of the consultative vote'. The same constitution provides that 'if it is expressly approved by the Roman Pontiff, the Final Document participates in the ordinary Magisterium of the Successor of Peter'. So the synod cannot change doctrine, because it is not a council and does not teach definitively; but its discernment is not theatre, and a final document approved by the pope becomes an act of his ordinary magisterium, which asks for religious submission under canon 752. The journalist confuses consultation with legislative power; the canonist confuses a consultative vote with an irrelevance.
questions.distractor: The canonist is right: because the vote is consultative, the final document is advice that a Catholic may set aside as opinion, and only a pope speaking ex cathedra or a council in session can produce teaching that binds anyone.
questions.correction: The distractor is the more common error among educated Catholics, and it fails on two texts it has not read. First, Episcopalis Communio expressly says that a final document approved by the Roman Pontiff 'participates in the ordinary Magisterium of the Successor of Peter', which is teaching that binds by canon 752 even though it is not a definition; the choice is therefore not between infallible definition and private opinion. Second, the distractor ignores that ordinary magisterial teaching of any kind asks for religious submission of intellect and will, as Ad Tuendam Fidem's third paragraph and canon 752 both state. Where the distractor is right is only in denying that a synod as such defines doctrine, and that point must be kept; the error is the slide from 'not a definition' to 'not teaching', which flattens the three grades of assent into two.

questions.prompt: A traditionalist website argues that because the Byzantine Church repudiated the union concluded at Florence in 1439, the Florentine decree on purgatory and on the Roman primacy was never 'received' and therefore never became binding teaching; a progressive website draws the opposite conclusion from the same history, that binding teaching is whatever the faithful end up accepting. Assess both arguments using Lumen Gentium 25 and Pastor Aeternus.
questions.answer: Both arguments make reception a condition of truth, which is the error the texts exclude. Pastor Aeternus says papal definitions are irreformable 'of themselves, and not by the consent of the church'; Lumen Gentium 25 says that to the Church's definitions 'the assent of the Church can never be wanting, on account of the activity of that same Holy Spirit', which describes a promised effect of the definition, not a precondition of its validity. Florence's decree of union was a genuine act of a council in union with the pope, and its doctrinal content on purgatory, the procession of the Spirit and the primacy stands on that authority; the collapse of the political union and the refusal of the Byzantine churches to accept it are historical facts about reception, not a tribunal that annuls the act. What the history does show is that reception is a real process, uneven, slow and sometimes failed, and that its failure is a signal to ask what went wrong, whether in the doctrine, in its formulation, or in the circumstances of its imposition.
questions.distractor: The traditionalist is right that reception is required, and the progressive is right about what reception means: a teaching becomes binding when the Church receives it, so Florence's decree never became binding in the East, and the same test explains why the Church's moral teaching on contraception is now doubtful, since a large majority do not receive it.
questions.correction: The distractor joins a correct premise to a false conclusion and then extends the false conclusion to a case that exposes it. Reception is indeed a real process, and the Church's own documents speak of it; but making it the criterion of truth inverts the relation the two texts establish, and it produces the absurd consequence that a definition's authority could be voted down by those it addresses, which is precisely what Pastor Aeternus denies and what Lumen Gentium 25 describes as impossible in the order of providence. The extension to moral teaching also confuses two things: the failure of many Catholics to accept a teaching is evidence about catechesis and about the state of the Church's life, not evidence about the truth of the teaching, and the documents that treat the sensus fidei (Lumen Gentium 12) insist that it cannot be equated with the majority opinion of the moment. The correct answer keeps reception as an event in the Church's history whose failures are instructive, not as a court of appeal above the magisterium.

questions.prompt: Two students argue about John Paul II's 1994 letter Ordinatio Sacerdotalis. The first says it cannot be infallible teaching because the pope did not speak ex cathedra and the letter is not a definition. The second says it is a dogma of divine faith in the strictest sense, on the same footing as the definition of 1854. Using the 1995 response of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith and Ad Tuendam Fidem, state what is settled and what is a matter of theological classification.
questions.answer: Settled: the teaching that priestly ordination is reserved to men is to be held definitively and is not open to dissent. Ordinatio Sacerdotalis states that 'the Church has no authority whatsoever to confer priestly ordination on women and that this judgment is to be definitively held by all the Church's faithful'; the 1995 response adds that the teaching 'has been preserved by the constant and universal Tradition of the Church and has been set forth infallibly by the ordinary and universal Magisterium', and that it is 'to be understood as belonging to the deposit of the faith'. The first student's premise is therefore false: a definition is not the only mode of infallible teaching, and Lumen Gentium 25 attributes infallibility to the body of bishops teaching definitively with Peter's successor. Open to theological analysis: whether the teaching belongs to the first paragraph of the Profession of Faith, truths divinely revealed and believed with divine faith, or to the second, truths definitively proposed because they are required for the faithful exposition of the deposit. The 1995 response speaks of the deposit; the standard commentary on Ad Tuendam Fidem places it in the second paragraph. That classification is argued, the obligation is not.
questions.distractor: The first student is right that infallibility requires an ex cathedra definition, so the letter is authoritative but reformable teaching that a Catholic may criticise in a theological journal; and the second student is right that if it were infallible it would have to be a dogma of divine faith, so the question is whether the pope has defined it.
questions.correction: The distractor holds two true premises and one false inference. It is true that Ordinatio Sacerdotalis is not an ex cathedra definition, and true that a definition would have to state whether its content is divinely revealed; false that infallibility is confined to definitions, which is the error the 1995 response was issued to correct and which Ad Tuendam Fidem's second paragraph presupposes by describing truths 'definitively proposed' that are not simply revealed. The distractor also mislocates the freedom: what a theologian may legitimately do is argue about the precise theological note and about how the arguments from Scripture and Tradition are best formulated, and the literature does exactly that; what no one may do is treat a teaching the Church has said is to be held definitively as one opinion among others, which is the practical conclusion the distractor invites.

units.title: Cases of Change and Non-Change: Capital Punishment, Slavery, Indulgences, Sacramental Validity and Liturgical Discipline

lessons.title: The death penalty: how 2267 moved from 'not excluded' to 'inadmissible'
lessons.explanation: Lesson 80 established that the Church's teaching on war has constants, criteria and prudential judgments, and lesson 63 that development must be shown rather than asserted; this lesson applies both to the one paragraph of the Catechism that has been revised under three popes. The 1992 text of 2267 acknowledged 'the traditional teaching of the Church' that legitimate public authority may punish malefactors with penalties 'not excluding, in cases of extreme gravity, the death penalty' where this is the only way of effectively defending human lives. The 1997 editio typica altera tightened the condition: where bloodless means suffice to defend lives and protect public order, 'public authority must limit itself to such means, because they better correspond to the concrete conditions of the common good and are more in conformity to the dignity of the human person'. John Paul II had already pushed the argument further in Evangelium Vitae 56, where he observed that the cases in which execution is 'an absolute necessity' are 'very rare, if not practically non-existent'. The 2018 revision, approved by Francis and presented by the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith on 1 August 2018, replaced the permission with a judgment: 'the Church teaches, in the light of the Gospel, that the death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person, and she works with determination for its abolition worldwide.' Three phrases in the new text do the argumentative work. 'In the light of the Gospel' locates the judgment in revelation rather than in sociology. 'Attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person' gives a reason of principle, not a calculation. 'Increasing awareness' and 'more effective systems of detention' supply the historical account of why the Church sees this now. The CDF's accompanying letter is explicit about the kind of change: the revision 'situates itself in continuity with the preceding Magisterium while bringing forth a coherent development of Catholic doctrine', and the new formulation 'expresses an authentic development of doctrine that is not in contradiction with the prior teachings of the Magisterium'. The letter then explains the earlier teaching by its setting: penalties were understood differently, and it was harder to guarantee that a criminal could not repeat his crime. What the letter does not do is tell the student which of two analyses to adopt, and the difference matters. On one reading, the constant is the dignity of the person and the change is the recognition that execution always attacks it, which makes the new judgment a development in moral doctrine with a claim about the act itself. On the other, the constant is the state's duty to defend the innocent and the change is the factual judgment that the duty can now be discharged without execution, which makes the new judgment a universally taught prudential conclusion. The magisterium has not adjudicated between these readings, and both are held by serious theologians; what it has excluded is the two errors that treat the question as settled in advance.
lessons.example: Read the three texts side by side and classify the clauses, because the change is visible only in the comparison. The 1992 paragraph has the structure of a permission with a condition: a right of public authority, a penalty not excluded, and the condition of necessity. The 1997 paragraph keeps the structure but reverses the presumption: bloodless means must be used where they suffice, and the reason given is the dignity of the person, which is a principle rather than a forecast. The 2018 paragraph drops the permission altogether and states the conclusion as teaching, with two grounds: the dignity that survives the worst crimes, and the changed penal and carceral situation. Now classify each element. The state's duty to defend its citizens is doctrine, and the 2018 letter expressly reaffirms it by citing 2265 and 2266. The judgment that the penalty is an attack on inviolability is a moral judgment proposed as binding, and the letter calls it a development of doctrine. The judgments about detention systems and about the purposes of punishment are empirical and historical, and they are the kind of premise a legislator can investigate. The practical conclusion for a reader is that the paragraph cannot be handled as a single undifferentiated claim: quoting 'inadmissible' without the reasons makes it sound like a slogan, and quoting the reasons without the conclusion makes it sound like a policy brief. The Church's own text holds them together, and the student's job is to show how.
lessons.question: A catechist says that the change in 2267 is not really a change at all, because the Church's principle about defending innocent life has never altered and the Catechism has merely applied it to modern circumstances. Is that an adequate account?
lessons.answer: It is half an account and it cannot explain the text. It is true that the principle has not altered, and the 2018 letter itself explains the earlier teaching by reference to a social context in which penal sanctions were understood differently. But an application that reverses a permission into a prohibition is not a neutral restatement: the 1992 Catechism said the penalty was not excluded, and the 2018 Catechism says it is inadmissible, and a reader who calls that 'merely' an application has removed the need for the Church to have said anything at all. The letter's own vocabulary is stronger than the catechist's: it speaks of 'a coherent development of Catholic doctrine' and 'an authentic development of doctrine', not of a prudential adjustment. What the catechist is right to resist is the opposite over-reading, that the Church once taught error; the letter excludes that too, saying the development 'is not in contradiction with the prior teachings'. The adequate account therefore has to do three things: name the constant, describe what changed, and say what kind of act the new judgment is, which is precisely what the letter does and what the catechist's formula skips.
lessons.distractor: It is a complete account: because the principle is unchanged and only the circumstances have changed, the new paragraph is a prudential judgment addressed to legislators, and a Catholic who concludes that in his country the old necessity still obtains may support retention of the penalty without departing from the Catechism.
lessons.correction: The distractor draws the conclusion that the 1997 text might have supported and that the 2018 text rules out. The current 2267 does not say that the penalty is inadmissible where alternatives are unavailable; it says that it is inadmissible because it attacks the inviolability and dignity of the person, which is a reason that does not vary with the availability of prisons. The distractor also misdescribes the act: a prudential judgment about means is one that Catholics may legitimately dispute, whereas the CDF letter presents this as 'an authentic development of doctrine', which asks for a different response. Where the distractor has a point is in insisting that legislators still have real work to do, since abolition has to be enacted, sequenced and secured, and the Church's teaching does not dictate a parliamentary timetable. That is the legitimate space, and it is narrower than the distractor claims: it concerns how abolition is achieved, not whether the penalty may be defended as a good.

depth.definitions: Capital punishment: the taking of life by public authority as a penalty for crime, distinguished from lethal force used in immediate defence against an aggressor (CCC 2265). Inadmissible: the term of the 2018 revision, stronger than 'impermissible in most cases' and weaker than a conciliar anathema, and used with a stated reason. Development of doctrine: the Church's growth in understanding of a truth she already holds, which the CDF letter invokes for this change. Prudential judgment: the assessment of how a principle applies to circumstances, which the Church assigns to those responsible for the common good. Intrinsically evil act: an act excluded by its object regardless of consequences, the framework of Veritatis Splendor 80. Penal purpose: the ends of punishment, which the 2018 letter describes as oriented 'above all to the rehabilitation and social reintegration of the criminal'. Prerequisites: the moral act (56), the development of doctrine (63), and the war lesson's three layers (80).
depth.mechanism: How does a permission become a prohibition without the Church contradicting herself? By the mechanism the tradition calls a development in continuity: a principle that was always held generates a new judgment when the conditions it presupposed are seen to have been doing silent work. In the 1992 text, the condition of necessity was not a formality; it was the load-bearing element, since the permission was justified by the state's inability otherwise to protect the innocent. Once the Church concludes that the inability no longer holds, and adds the deepening conviction that the dignity of the person survives the worst crime, the permission has nothing left to stand on. The 2018 letter states both halves of that movement, the change in penal practice and the clearer awareness of dignity, and describes the result as development rather than reversal. What makes this more than a policy change is the reason given: 'an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person' is a judgment about the act's object, not about its consequences, and judgments about objects are the kind that the Church treats as doctrine. What keeps it from being a simple reversal is the letter's insistence that the earlier teaching was intelligible in its context and is not now to be repudiated as error. The mechanism is therefore a narrowing: the space in which the older permission could operate has been closed by the Church's own deepening grasp of what the permission was always for.
depth.secondExample: Take the case the paragraph does not cover, because the boundary is where students go wrong: a gunman in a school, or a prisoner who has seized a guard's weapon and is killing other inmates. Here the relevant text is not 2267 but 2265, which teaches that legitimate defence may involve the taking of an aggressor's life when it is the only way to protect innocent lives, and that the act is not to be judged as murder when it is proportionate to the good defended. The difference is not merely procedural. Capital punishment is inflicted after capture, by a judicial act, on a person who is no longer attacking anyone; lethal force in defence is used against an aggressor in the act, and its justification runs out when the threat does. That is why a Catholic who accepts the 2018 revision can also accept that a police officer may shoot a man who is firing into a crowd, and why the two positions are not in tension. The transferable distinction is between the object of the act, which is defence of the innocent, and the object of the penalty, which is retribution and the protection of order by judicial killing. Applying it to a hard case, such as a state that has collapsed and holds a captured mass murderer with no secure prison, shows the limits of the analysis: the duty of defence remains, the ordinary means are absent, and the honest conclusion is that the Church's teaching has made the permissible route exceedingly narrow without pretending that providence guarantees easy cases.
depth.mistake: The progressive error says the Church has finally admitted that its earlier teaching was wrong, and therefore that moral doctrine is simply the record of the Church catching up with enlightened opinion. Its diagnostic is that it cannot explain the 2018 letter's repeated claim of continuity, and it makes the Church's future teaching unpredictable in principle, since on this account anything may be reversed. The conservative error says nothing has changed, since the principle is the same and the paragraph is a prudential judgment; its diagnostic is that it must paraphrase away the word 'inadmissible' and ignore the letter's phrase 'authentic development of doctrine'. A third error, common among lawyers and journalists, treats the paragraph as a legislative act that binds states, when it binds consciences and directs the Church's advocacy, and the enactment of abolition remains a political task with its own prudential arguments. The three errors can be diagnosed with one question each: what is the constant, what is the change, and what grade of act states the change? A reader who answers all three has the lesson; a reader who answers one and stops has an ideology.
depth.application: Task (nonblocking, 50 minutes): write a one-page briefing for a Catholic legislator in a state that retains the penalty, with four sections. Section one, THE TEXTS: quote the operative sentence of the current 2267 and one sentence each from the 1997 revision and Evangelium Vitae 56, with dates. Section two, WHAT IS TAUGHT: state the judgment, its reason, and the grade of act, citing the CDF letter's phrase about development of doctrine. Section three, WHAT IS OPEN: list two questions a legislator may legitimately argue about, for example the sequencing of abolition or the treatment of prisoners serving whole-life sentences, and say why each is prudential. Section four, WHAT IS NOT OPEN: state one position that would contradict the teaching and name the error it embodies. Rubric: section two must not use the phrase 'the Church says' without a document; section three must include at least one argument you find persuasive but do not adopt; and no section may present the 1992 text as the current position. A briefing that quotes only the 1992 Catechism has failed, and so has one that quotes only the word 'inadmissible' without its reason.
depth.summary: Catechism 2267 moved in three steps: the 1992 text did not exclude the death penalty where it was the only way to defend lives, the 1997 revision required bloodless means where they suffice, and the 2018 revision, with the CDF letter of 1 August 2018, teaches that the penalty is inadmissible because it attacks the inviolability and dignity of the person, describing the change as a coherent development of doctrine in continuity with the earlier magisterium. The constant is the state's duty to defend the innocent and the dignity of the person; the change is the recognition that execution attacks that dignity and that modern detention can discharge the duty. What remains legitimately arguable is the theological analysis of the change, whether the judgment concerns the act's object or the circumstances, and the political means of abolition; what is excluded is treating the teaching as a policy preference or the earlier magisterium as having taught error.

lessons.title: Slavery: the hardest case in the history of moral doctrine
lessons.explanation: Lesson 86 gave a case where the Church moved from a narrow permission to a prohibition and described the movement as development; this lesson takes the case where the same movement occurred but where the Church's own record makes the description much harder to sustain. Begin with what is not in dispute. The practice of slavery was tolerated for centuries in societies the Church inhabited, and Christians participated in it, including clergy and religious institutes. Papal acts of the fifteenth century granted rights of conquest and trade over non-Christian peoples, and those grants were later invoked in defence of the Atlantic trade. Theologians elaborated defences of servitude, drawing on Aristotle's account of natural slavery and on arguments about capture in a just war. In 1866 the Holy Office, in a reply approved by Pius IX, held that slavery considered in itself and as such was not contrary to natural and divine law, while condemning the traffic in slaves. Against that record stands a counter-current that was always present and eventually prevailed. Paul III's Sublimis Deus (1537) condemned the enslavement of the Indians and affirmed their capacity for faith; Benedict XIV's Immensa Pastorum (1741) condemned the enslavement of indigenous peoples in the Portuguese and Spanish dominions; Gregory XVI's In Supremo Apostolatus (1839) denounced the slave trade as inhuman and contrary to the dignity of the human person; Leo XIII returned to the question in In Plurimis (1888). The Second Vatican Council then stated the conclusion in terms that admit no qualification: Gaudium et Spes 27 lists 'slavery, prostitution, the selling of women and children' among the infamies that dishonour the Creator and violate human dignity, and Veritatis Splendor 80 cites that list as its example of acts which 'per se and in themselves, independently of circumstances, are always seriously wrong by reason of their object'. John Paul II, in the Lenten liturgy of 12 March 2000, asked forgiveness in the name of the Church for the infidelities of her children across history, and Novo Millennio Ineunte 6 describes that act of purification of memory. Three levels must now be distinguished with more care than anywhere else in this level. The principle that every human person is made in the image of God and cannot be owned is taught throughout, and it is defined in substance. The modern judgment that slavery is intrinsically evil is authoritative moral teaching, taught as binding in a council and an encyclical, but it has not been proposed in a conciliar definition with an anathema, and it should be described as definitive moral teaching rather than as a dogma. What is legitimately debated is narrower and more uncomfortable: whether the fifteenth-century grants carried any doctrinal content or were permissions with no teaching weight; how the 1866 reply is to be classified given that its abstract thesis is the one the modern magisterium denies; and whether the honest name for the change is development or correction, given that John Noonan's study of the case, A Church That Can and Cannot Change (2005), argues that some earlier papal acts were simply wrong.
lessons.example: Take the modern texts and run the analysis of the moral object, because that is where the case becomes teachable. Gaudium et Spes 27 places slavery in a list of acts that violate the human person, alongside torture, arbitrary imprisonment and the selling of women and children. Veritatis Splendor 80 uses that list to illustrate its thesis about intrinsically evil acts: 'there exist acts which per se and in themselves, independently of circumstances, are always seriously wrong by reason of their object'. Now ask what the object of slaveholding is. It is not the labour of another, which can be owed under a contract or a sentence; it is the treatment of a person as property, which is to say the denial of the very capacity for ownership that defines a person in the order of creation. That is why the modern judgment cannot be reduced to a conclusion about circumstances: no improvement in the conditions of slaves, no benevolence of a master, and no economic necessity alters the object, because the object is dominion over a person. Once the object is identified, the older theological defences can be diagnosed rather than merely deplored. The appeal to Aristotle confused a person's servile function with a person's nature; the appeal to capture in a just war confused a penalty with a status, since a just penalty is limited and a status is hereditary and total; and the appeal to Scripture read the curse of Ham as a charter for an institution the text does not establish. The exercise is not to score points against the tradition but to see how a true principle can be obstructed by a false anthropology, which is the pattern the whole lesson turns on.
lessons.question: A student writes that because the Church's teaching on slavery changed, and because the change was not a development of a definition but a reversal of a position popes had approved, the honest conclusion is that the Church's moral teaching is fallible in its substance and may change again on other questions. How should this be answered?
lessons.answer: By conceding the historical facts and refusing the inference, and by being precise about what kind of act was reversed. The facts are as the student states: papal grants were issued, theologians defended servitude, and the 1866 reply of the Holy Office approved by Pius IX held that slavery in itself was not against natural law. But the acts in question were not definitions: they were permissions, prudential judgments about legal institutions, and in the case of the 1866 reply a doctrinal judgment of a congregation on an abstract thesis that rested on a theory of dominion. The Church's claim about herself is that definitions of faith and morals are irreformable, not that every act of every dicastery is. A correction of a non-definitive judgment is therefore compatible with the Church's claims, and it is the only description that fits the evidence. What the case does show is that the Church's teaching office can be obstructed by a false anthropology, and that the Church's growth in moral understanding has sometimes required repentance rather than the retrieval of a formula. That is a more demanding conclusion than the student's, because it does not let anyone say that anything may change: the principle that generated the correction is now seen to exclude the practice absolutely, which is why the modern teaching is stated as intrinsic and not as provisional.
lessons.distractor: The student is right, and the case proves more than he claims: since the Church's moral teaching on slavery was wrong for centuries and was corrected only under social pressure, the same must be true of other teachings that rest on the same kind of natural-law argument, so a Catholic is entitled to treat them as provisional until the Church catches up.
lessons.correction: The distractor accepts a true description of the past and builds a false principle on it, and the false principle is the one this whole level exists to expose. It moves from 'a non-definitive act was corrected' to 'the teaching is provisional', which ignores the distinction between the grades of act that Ad Tuendam Fidem and Lumen Gentium 25 establish, and it converts a single hard case into a general licence. It also misdescribes the causality: the correction was driven by the Church's own premises about creation and redemption, argued by figures such as Las Casas and the missionaries who appealed to the Holy See, and the social pressure the distractor invokes followed the argument as often as it caused it. Where the student's original formulation was better than the distractor is that it at least named the difficulty, which is real: the Church's record includes acts that later teaching contradicts, and the honest response is to classify those acts precisely rather than to deny them or to generalise from them.

depth.definitions: Servitude: the legal and social institution by which a person is owned, distinguished from other forms of bonded labour by the permanence and heritability of the status. Natural slavery: the Aristotelian thesis that some persons are fitted by nature to be ruled, used by some theologians to defend the institution and rejected by the modern magisterium's anthropology. Just title: the argument that enslavement could be legitimate through capture in a just war, birth, or sale, which the modern teaching excludes. Intrinsic evil: an act wrong by reason of its object regardless of consequences, the category Veritatis Splendor 80 applies to slavery by citing Gaudium et Spes 27. Non-definitive act: an act of the magisterium that teaches authoritatively without proposing definitively, and that can therefore be corrected without a definition being reversed. Purification of memory: John Paul II's phrase in Novo Millennio Ineunte 6 for the Church's confession of the sins of her children. Prerequisites: the moral object (56), the development of doctrine (63), and the grades of assent (85).
depth.mechanism: How does a true principle coexist for centuries with a false conclusion? Not by hypocrisy alone, but by the mediation of an anthropology. The principle that the human person is the image of God and cannot be reduced to a thing was never denied; what was supplied, and what did the damage, was an account of dominion that sorted humanity into those capable of self-rule and those naturally subject, and a legal theory that made capture, birth and sale into just titles. Once that mediation is in place, the principle can be affirmed while the practice is defended, and the defence will even generate pastoral solicitude for the slave's soul, which is the most painful feature of the record. The correction occurs when the mediation is dismantled: when the anthropology of natural slavery is rejected, when the just titles are examined and found to be rationalisations, and when the Church's own experience of enslaved and freed Christians makes the contradiction visible. The mechanism is therefore not the replacement of a principle but the removal of an obstruction, and it has a moral cost, because the obstruction was held in place by the Church's own institutions and by her silence. That is why the modern magisterium speaks in the register of repentance as well as of doctrine, and why John Paul II's 12 March 2000 liturgy belongs to the argument rather than to the decoration.
depth.secondExample: Take the papal documents of the nineteenth century and watch the trajectory within them, because that is a different exercise from analysing the moral object. In Supremo Apostolatus (1839) condemns the slave trade, addresses the faithful on the inhumanity of the traffic, and urges the clergy to work for its abolition; it does not declare slaveholding as such to be always and everywhere wrong, and its argument is framed by the duty of Christians to treat slaves with justice and charity. In Plurimis (1888) welcomes the abolition in Brazil and treats the institution as incompatible with the Gospel, while still addressing the duties of masters and the care of freed persons. Gaudium et Spes 27 then lists slavery among the acts that violate human dignity, and Veritatis Splendor 80 makes the list the paradigm of intrinsic evil. Read in sequence, the documents show a narrowing that is visible in their own wording: from condemning the trade, to welcoming abolition, to classifying the institution as an infamy. Three things can be said about that sequence with confidence. It is real, and it is not the invention of later historians. It is not a definition, so the technical language of dogma is out of place. And it is not neutral: each step made the next one harder to avoid, which is what a genuine development looks like from the inside. The same exercise can be repeated with the Church's teaching on torture or on the treatment of indigenous peoples, and the pattern recurs.
depth.mistake: The first error is the apologetic one: insisting that the Church always condemned slavery in principle, so that the papal grants, the theological defences and the 1866 reply were aberrations without weight. Its diagnostic is that it cannot explain why the corrections were necessary, why John Paul II asked forgiveness, or why the 1866 reply exists at all; and it leaves the Church unable to say what she repented of. The second error is the sceptical one: generalising from this case to the conclusion that all moral teaching is provisional, which ignores the distinction between non-definitive acts that were corrected and definitions that are irreformable, and which cannot explain why the modern judgment is stated as intrinsic rather than as a temporary policy. The third error is the scholarly evasion that calls the earlier acts 'merely disciplinary', which is too quick: the fifteenth-century grants conferred real rights, the 1866 reply made a doctrinal claim in the abstract, and calling all of that discipline is a way of avoiding the question. The discipline required here is the hardest in the level: to state the record without euphemism, to classify each act by its grade, and to describe the change with the word that fits, which in this case is not only development but also correction and repentance.
depth.application: Task (nonblocking, 60 minutes): build a five-row document table for 1537, 1839, 1866, 1965 and 1993, with columns for WHAT IS CONDEMNED, WHAT IS PRESUPPOSED, WHAT GRADE OF ACT, and WHAT THE TEXT DOES NOT SAY. Use Sublimis Deus, In Supremo Apostolatus, the 1866 reply of the Holy Office, Gaudium et Spes 27 and Veritatis Splendor 80. Model entry for 1965: 'Condemned: slavery as an infamy violating human dignity. Presupposed: the anthropology of the person as image of God and as subject, not object, of dominion. Grade: conciliar moral teaching, definitive in substance, not a definition with an anathema. Does not say: that every form of penal labour or debt bondage is slavery in the same sense.' Then write a 150-word paragraph answering the question 'was this development or correction?', using each row as evidence and refusing to use either word without a reason attached. Rubric: the table must include at least one entry whose grade you cannot settle, and the paragraph must name one thing the Church has repented of and one thing she has not changed.
depth.summary: Slavery is the hardest case because the Church's record includes papal grants, theological defences and an 1866 reply of the Holy Office holding that servitude in itself was not against natural law, alongside a counter-current running from Sublimis Deus (1537) through In Supremo Apostolatus (1839) and In Plurimis (1888) to Gaudium et Spes 27 and Veritatis Splendor 80, which class slavery among the acts always wrong by reason of their object. The principle of human dignity was constant; what failed was the anthropology of natural slavery and the theory of just titles that mediated it, and the correction required repentance as well as argument. The modern judgment is authoritative and definitive in substance without being a conciliar definition, and the acts that were reversed were non-definitive permissions and judgments, which is why the case does not license the conclusion that doctrine is provisional. The discipline is to state the record without euphemism and to classify each act by its grade.

Bottom layer, a timeline of the practice with two rows: the record of complicity (fifteenth-century papal grants, clerical slaveholding, theological defences, the 1866 reply of the Holy Office) and the counter-current (Sublimis Deus 1537, Immensa Pastorum 1741, In Supremo Apostolatus 1839, In Plurimis 1888).

A wedge labelled CORRECTION driven between the constant and the practice, splitting the slab, with the dates 1965 (Gaudium et Spes 27) and 1993 (Veritatis Splendor 80) marked where the slabs fall away, and a side caption from Novo Millennio Ineunte 6 on the purification of memory.

A side box headed CLASSIFY, with three rows: DEFINED (the dignity of the person), DEFINITIVE MORAL TEACHING (slavery is intrinsically evil), DEBATED (whether the fifteenth-century grants carried doctrinal content, how the 1866 reply is classified, whether the change is best called development or correction).

lessons.title: Indulgences: what Trent defined, what Paul VI reformed, and where the abuse lay
lessons.explanation: Lesson 38 treated penance and the shape of conversion, and lesson 63 the tests of development; this lesson takes the doctrine that the Reformation was fought over and that most Catholics now understand least. Begin with the distinction the whole subject rests on, because without it nothing else can be stated correctly. Sin forgiven in the sacrament of penance is forgiven as to its guilt, and there remains what the tradition calls the temporal punishment due to sin: the disorder, the attachment, the damage to oneself and to others that forgiveness does not automatically repair. Trent's doctrine of satisfaction in Session 14 belongs here, and so does the Catechism's definition: 'an indulgence is a remission before God of the temporal punishment due to sins whose guilt has already been forgiven, which the faithful Christian who is duly disposed gains under certain prescribed conditions through the action of the Church which, as the minister of redemption, dispenses and applies with authority the treasury of the satisfactions of Christ and the saints' (CCC 1471, quoting Paul VI). The practice grew slowly and by accretion: the penitential discipline of the early Church, the intercession of confessors and martyrs for the reconciled, the commutation of canonical penances in the tariff books, the crusade indulgence proclaimed at Clermont in 1095, the Jubilee of 1300, and the formulation of the treasury of merits in Clement VI's bull Unigenitus of 1343. By the sixteenth century the practice was entangled with finance and with a theology of quantification that nobody had authorised. Trent's decree of 4 December 1563 responded on two levels at once. Doctrinally it taught that 'the power of conferring indulgences was granted by Christ to the Church', that their use is 'most salutary to the Christian people' and is to be 'retained in the Church', and it anathematised those who call them useless or deny the power to grant them. Practically it required moderation, ordered that 'all base and illicit bargains' be wholly abolished, and charged bishops with correcting abuses. What Trent did not do was define the treasury in the terms of the bull of 1343, define the measure of any indulgence, or settle the precise mode of application to the dead. The modern reform came from Paul VI. Indulgentiarum Doctrina (1 January 1967) restated the definition in the terms the Catechism now uses, abolished the reckoning in days and years for partial indulgences in favour of a measure based on the act and the charity of the one performing it, insisted that no indulgence can be gained without conversion and that the treasury 'should certainly not be imagined as the sum total of material goods accumulated in the course of the centuries' but is the infinite value of Christ's expiation and merits together with the prayers and good works of the saints, and reduced and reorganised the grants in the Enchiridion Indulgentiarum. Three levels therefore have to be kept apart: the defined doctrine of the Church's power, the authoritative theology of the treasury and of temporal punishment, and the disciplinary norms that govern particular grants and may change at will.
lessons.example: Take the question a penitent actually asks: if Christ's sacrifice is infinite and complete, what can an indulgence add? The answer requires three distinctions. First, between sufficiency and application: Trent's doctrine of justification denies that anything is lacking in Christ's satisfaction, and the Church's dispensing of the treasury is an application of what Christ has won, not a supplement to it, which is why the Catechism describes the Church as acting 'as the minister of redemption'. Second, between guilt and the disorder that remains: a forgiven adulterer is reconciled, and the habits of mind, the harm done and the attachments that produced the act are not undone by the words of absolution, which is what the tradition calls temporal punishment and what the penitential discipline of the early Church addressed through works of satisfaction. Third, between the Church's intercession and a mechanism: an indulgence is granted through the Church's authoritative intervention and presupposes the recipient's conversion, which is why Paul VI insists that the order of charity is preserved and that the grant cannot be acquired without a sincere change of mind. Put those together and the penitent's question has an answer that is neither a denial of the cross nor a commercial transaction: the Church, by the power of binding and loosing, applies to a converted sinner the merits of Christ and the communion of the saints so that the healing and reparation that sin made necessary may be completed. The answer also explains why indulgences are attached to prayer, pilgrimage, almsgiving and works of mercy, since those are the acts in which the conversion is exercised.
lessons.question: A catechist says that indulgences are a mediaeval accretion with no basis in the Gospel, that Trent defended them only because it had to, and that the 1967 reform effectively abolished them while keeping the word. Which parts of this are true, and what is the accurate account?
lessons.answer: Almost nothing is accurate, and the true parts are not the ones the catechist intends. The basis in the Gospel is the power of binding and loosing given to Peter and to the disciples (Matthew 16:19; 18:18; John 20:23), which Trent cites as the foundation of the Church's authority to grant indulgences, together with the communion of saints in which no member lives for himself. The mediaeval development is real, and it is what the Church means by the growth of a practice in the light of the deposit; the abuses that grew with it were also real, and Trent condemned them in the same decree that defended the doctrine. Trent did not defend indulgences reluctantly: it taught that the use is 'most salutary' and to be retained, and it anathematised those who deny the power. The 1967 reform did not abolish the practice but restated its doctrine, abolished the arithmetic of days and years, and reordered the grants; the Enchiridion Indulgentiarum remains the Church's book of norms, and the Catechism retains the doctrine at 1471 to 1479. What can be conceded is that the practice is not of divine institution in its concrete forms, and that its history includes exploitation on a scale that occasioned the Reformation.
lessons.distractor: The catechist is broadly right: indulgences rest on the mediaeval theory of a treasury of merits, which is a theological opinion rather than doctrine, and since the 1967 reform removed the days and years and reduced the grants, the honest description is that the Church has quietly retired the practice while retaining the word for pastoral reasons.
lessons.correction: The distractor commits two errors that pull in opposite directions and cancel each other. It calls the treasury a theological opinion, which understates the defined doctrine: what Trent defined is the Church's power to grant indulgences and their salutary character, and the treasury is the theological account of how that power operates, held consistently from Clement VI through Paul VI, which is more than an opinion though less than a definition. It then treats the 1967 reform as a retirement, which overstates what a disciplinary act can do: Paul VI restated the doctrine in the first norms of Indulgentiarum Doctrina, described the treasury in his own words, and left the practice in place with a reformed set of grants. The distractor's appeal to honesty about history is better served by the accurate account, which concedes the abuses and the accretion while keeping the grades straight: defined power, authoritative theology, changeable discipline, and a history that includes both corruption and reform.

depth.definitions: Indulgence: the remission before God of the temporal punishment due to sins whose guilt has been forgiven, gained through the Church's authoritative application of the treasury (CCC 1471). Temporal punishment: the disorder and reparation that remain after guilt is forgiven, distinguished from eternal punishment. Treasury of the Church: the infinite value of Christ's expiation and merits together with the prayers and good works of the saints, which Clement VI's Unigenitus (1343) formulated and Paul VI re-described in Indulgentiarum Doctrina. Plenary and partial: an indulgence remitting all or part of the temporal punishment (Indulgentiarum Doctrina, norm 2). Suffrage: the Church's intercession for the dead, which is the mode of applying indulgences to them, distinguished from absolution. Base and illicit bargains: Trent's phrase for the financial abuses it ordered abolished in the decree of 4 December 1563. Prerequisites: penance and satisfaction (38), the communion of saints and purgatory (67), and development (63).
depth.mechanism: Why does the Church's grant do anything at all? The mechanism is the communion of saints operating through the power of the keys. In the Church's understanding, the satisfaction offered by Christ is infinite, and the satisfactions of the saints are real because they are members of Christ and act in him; the Church, holding the keys, may apply that treasury to a penitent who is converted but still marked by the consequences of sin. Three constraints keep the mechanism from becoming magic. The first is the recipient's disposition: Paul VI's norms require that the person be duly disposed, and for a plenary indulgence that all attachment to sin, even venial, be absent, which is why the grant is not a transaction but an intensification of conversion. The second is the Church's own subordination: the minister of redemption dispenses what Christ has won, and the Catechism's language of 'applies with authority' is deliberately not the language of production. The third is the medicinal character of the punishment itself: temporal punishment is not a debt owed to a wrathful God but the disorder sin leaves, so the remission of it is intelligible as part of the healing the sacrament begins. Once the mechanism is stated this way, the historical abuses become intelligible too: they all consisted in detaching one element from the whole, either the grant from conversion, or the treasury from Christ, or the measure from the mystery.
depth.secondExample: Reconstruct 1517 and classify, because the historical case is the best test of whether the distinctions have been learned. The indulgence in question was granted for the rebuilding of Saint Peter's, preached in Germany under an arrangement that involved the archbishop of Mainz's debts and a banking house, and preached by men whose rhetoric suggested that a payment secured release from punishment, and that the souls in purgatory could be freed by the grant. Now sort the elements. The doctrine of the Church's power to grant indulgences is not the abuse: it was already taught, and Trent later defined it. The attachment of almsgiving to a grant is not in itself the abuse: the Church has always joined indulgences to works of mercy, and Paul VI's norms retain almsgiving among the works to which grants may be attached. What was abusive was the preaching, which (a) obscured that guilt must be forgiven in the sacrament before any question of temporal punishment arises, (b) implied that a financial contribution was the price of the grant rather than one of its conditions, and (c) presented the application to the dead as though it were an absolution under the Church's control rather than a suffrage. Luther's ninety-five theses attacked the third and the second with force and the first with less precision, and Trent's decree answered all three by defining the power, requiring moderation, abolishing base bargains, and leaving the abuses to the bishops. The lesson of the case is that a doctrine can be true and its preaching corrupt, and that reform in the Church has usually had to distinguish the two under pressure.
depth.mistake: Three errors recur. The first is the polemical one: 'the Church sold forgiveness', which confuses the remission of temporal punishment with the forgiveness of guilt and ignores the fact that the sacrament of penance, not the indulgence, is where guilt is forgiven. Its diagnostic is that it cannot explain why Trent's definition begins from sins 'whose guilt has already been forgiven'. The second is the sceptical one: 'indulgences are an invention', which has to explain away the power of the keys, the practice of the early Church's penitential discipline and the communion of saints, and which usually rests on the assumption that any development is an invention. The third is the internal Catholic one, and it is the most common in parishes: the arithmetic of days and years, as though an indulgence were a quantity of time in purgatory, which the 1967 reform abolished precisely because the quantification obscured the nature of the grant. A fourth, subtler error is the assumption that a plenary indulgence works automatically once the conditions are performed externally, which forgets the requirement of detachment from sin and turns a work of charity into a technique. The diagnostic for all four is the same question: is this claim about the forgiveness of guilt, about the remission of temporal punishment, or about the conditions and measure of a grant? Only the second is the subject of the doctrine, and only the third can be reformed by discipline.
depth.application: Task (nonblocking, 45 minutes): draft a correct parish announcement of a plenary indulgence for a feast day, in no more than 150 words, and then add a separate note of 100 words headed WHAT THIS DOES NOT MEAN. The announcement must state: the grant and its occasion, the conditions (sacramental confession, communion, prayer for the pope's intentions, and detachment from all attachment to sin, per Indulgentiarum Doctrina norm 7), the fact that the indulgence concerns temporal punishment and not the forgiveness of guilt, and the possibility of applying it to the dead by way of suffrage. The note must correct two misreadings, one of which you have actually heard. Rubric: no monetary amount may appear anywhere; the phrase 'remits sin' may not appear; every claim must be traceable to the Catechism 1471-1479 or to a numbered norm of Indulgentiarum Doctrina. Then compare your text with a real parish bulletin or online announcement and list every divergence, marking each as doctrinal, disciplinary or rhetorical. A draft that promises the release of a named soul from purgatory has failed, and so has one that omits the conditions.
depth.summary: An indulgence is the remission before God of the temporal punishment due to sins whose guilt has already been forgiven, gained through the Church's authoritative application of the treasury of Christ's satisfactions and the saints' (CCC 1471). Trent's decree of 4 December 1563 defined that the power was granted by Christ to the Church, that the use is most salutary and to be retained, and it ordered base bargains abolished and abuses corrected; Paul VI's Indulgentiarum Doctrina (1967) restated the doctrine, abolished the reckoning in days and years, re-described the treasury, and left the grants to be governed by the Enchiridion. The defined doctrine is the Church's power, the theology of the treasury and of temporal punishment is authoritative teaching, and the norms governing particular grants are discipline. The characteristic errors are confusing the indulgence with the forgiveness of guilt, treating the practice as a late invention, quantifying it in days and years, and imagining that the grant works without conversion.
