lessons.title: Sacramental validity: matter, form, intention, and the 2020 note on 'We baptise you'
lessons.explanation: Lesson 37 treated the sacraments of initiation and lesson 88 showed how a doctrine can be true while its practice is corrupt; this lesson takes the question underneath both, which is what makes a sacrament exist at all. The Church's answer has a technical vocabulary and a conciliar basis. Trent, in Session 7 (1547), defined against the Reformers that there are seven sacraments instituted by Christ, that they confer grace ex opere operato, that is, by the act performed and not by the faith or worthiness of the recipient or minister, and that the minister must have at least the intention of doing what the Church does: 'if anyone says that in ministers, when they effect and confer the sacraments, there is not required the intention at least of doing what the Church does, let him be anathema.' The same session anathematised the claim that a minister in mortal sin does not confer the sacrament. From those canons the Schools derived the elements that have to be present for validity: suitable matter, the determinate form, a minister with the required power, and the intention of doing what the Church does, together with a subject capable of receiving. The minister acts not in his own name but in the person of Christ, which is why the Church has always insisted, and Trent defined in Session 7 canon 8, that the efficacy is Christ's and the minister's sanctity is neither necessary nor sufficient. Validity must then be distinguished from two neighbours. Liceity concerns whether a sacrament may lawfully be celebrated in these circumstances, so that a valid baptism by a schismatic or an excommunicated priest can be valid and gravely illicit. Fruitfulness concerns the grace actually received, which depends on the disposition of the recipient and can be blocked by obstinacy. The 2020 case shows the machinery working on the element most easily overlooked. The Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith was asked whether baptism conferred with the formula 'We baptise you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit' is valid, and answered that it is not, adding that those so baptised must be baptised in forma absoluta rather than conditionally. Its doctrinal note explains that the faith of the Church is expressed in the sacramental act not only by the minister's intention but also by the formula and the matter, and that the minister does not act in his own name but in the person of Christ who acts in his Church; the change from 'I' to 'We' makes the community, rather than Christ through his minister, the subject of the act, and therefore alters the sign. The lesson's structure follows: validity is about the sign, and the sign has parts.
lessons.example: Take an emergency and vary one element at a time. A nurse with no religious belief finds a newborn not breathing, pours water over the head while saying 'I baptise you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit', intending to do what the Church does in baptising, and the child dies. Is the child baptised? Yes. The matter is water, the form is exact, the minister may be any person in case of necessity, and the intention required is not faith but the will to perform the rite the Church performs, which the nurse has been taught to supply. Now vary the elements. Remove the water and use sand: no sacrament, because the matter is not suitable. Keep the water and change the formula to 'We baptise you': no sacrament, on the 2020 response, because the form is defective. Keep the water and formula but have the nurse intending to perform a merely social gesture: no sacrament, because the intention is absent, though the Church's practice is to presume the intention where the rite is performed. Keep the water, the formula and the intention but make the subject an adult who is already baptised: no sacrament, because baptism imprints a character and cannot be repeated. Finally, keep everything and have the minister be a priest who has abandoned the ministry: the sacrament is valid and the celebration gravely illicit, which is the distinction Trent's canon 12 protects. The exercise is mechanical on purpose, because the point is that validity is not a judgment about sincerity, orthodoxy or worthiness but about whether the sign Christ instituted was performed.
lessons.question: A parish discovers that a visiting cleric baptised forty people with the formula 'We baptise you'. The parish priest proposes to baptise all forty conditionally, since conditional baptism is the Church's way of handling doubtful cases. Is that the right response, and what follows for the forty?
lessons.answer: It is not, and the 2020 response is explicit. The congregation was asked two questions, whether such baptism is valid and whether the persons must be baptised absolutely, and it answered that the baptism is invalid and that they must be baptised in forma absoluta. Conditional baptism presupposes a genuine doubt about whether a sacrament occurred; here there is no doubt, because the defect is in the form and the Church has declared the consequence. Absolute baptism is therefore required, with the correct formula and the same intention the Church has always asked of any minister. Two further consequences follow, and they are the ones a parish usually forgets. First, the records must be corrected, not annotated with a note that leaves the original entry standing as a baptismal certificate. Second, anything that presupposes baptism must be examined: confirmations, first communions, marriages celebrated with a defective baptismal record, and above all ordinations, since orders presuppose baptism, and a priest ordained on an invalid baptism is not a priest. The pastoral handling should be prompt and without alarm, since the remedy is short and the sacrament is not in doubt once properly conferred.
lessons.distractor: Conditional baptism is the correct response, because the Church never repeats a sacrament and a conditional form protects both possibilities: if the first rite was valid the condition fails and nothing happens, and if it was invalid the baptism takes effect. The forty should be told that their baptismal certificates remain valid in canon law, since the minister intended to do what the Church does and the defect was merely verbal.
lessons.correction: The distractor's logic is sound in a case of doubt and inapplicable here, which is exactly the error the 2020 response was issued to prevent. Conditional baptism is for facts that cannot be established, such as whether water was used or whether a rite was performed at all; it is not a general insurance policy, and using it where the Church has declared the rite invalid obscures the very defect that has to be corrected. The distractor also invokes the minister's intention in the wrong place: the intention was present, and the defect was in the form, so the argument that 'he meant well' does not touch the question of validity, since the sign is constituted by matter and form as well as by intention. The claim about the certificates is the most damaging part, because it leaves forty people believing they are baptised when the Church has said they are not, and it defers the examination of dependent sacraments, including orders, which is where the real harm would lie.

depth.definitions: Validity: the sacramental sign's existence, determined by matter, form, minister, intention and subject. Liceity: the lawfulness of a celebration, which can be violated while validity remains. Ex opere operato: the efficacy of the sacrament by the act performed, defined at Trent Session 7 against the claim that faith in the recipient is what confers grace. Matter and form: the sensible element and the determinate words, both required for the sign. Intention: the minister's will at least to do what the Church does, distinguished from his faith or worth. Character: the indelible mark conferred by baptism, confirmation and order, which is why those sacraments cannot be repeated. In forma absoluta: without a condition, the mode the 2020 response requires for those baptised with the altered formula. Prerequisites: the sacraments of initiation (37), the ministerial priesthood (83), and the doctrine of the sacramental sign (44).
depth.mechanism: Why does the form of words matter so much, and why does a pronoun decide whether a person is baptised? Because a sacrament is a sign, and a sign is constituted by its elements, not by the intention behind it. The 2020 note states the principle in a sentence: the faith of the Church is expressed in the sacramental act not only by the minister's intention but also by the formula and the matter. The words are not a label attached to a ritual already complete; they are the element by which the rite signifies what it does, and the Church's use of the first person singular is not a stylistic preference but the linguistic form of the claim that Christ baptises through his minister. Change the subject of the verb and the sign now signifies a different act, the community baptising itself, even if everyone present means the same thing by it. This is why the Church can be strict without being legalistic: the strictness is fidelity to the sign, and the sign is what carries the grace. The same mechanism explains the Church's tolerance elsewhere. She accepts baptism by any person, in any language, with any added ceremonies, because those variations do not alter the constitutive elements; she rejects an altered formula, an unsuitable matter, or the absence of intention, because those do alter them. The distinction is not between important and unimportant words but between constitutive and accidental ones, and the 2020 response is a lesson in how to tell them apart.
depth.secondExample: The Donatist controversy is the historical test case, and it is worth working through because it isolates the element the 2020 case does not concern. In the fourth century a party in North Africa held that the validity of a sacrament depended on the worthiness of the minister, so that baptisms and orders conferred by a bishop who had handed over the Scriptures under persecution were null, and those baptised by him had to be rebaptised. Augustine argued against them from the Church's practice and from the nature of the sacrament: the minister acts in the person of Christ, and the sacrament belongs to Christ and the Church, not to the man who administers it, so a wicked minister confers what a holy one confers. Trent's canon 12 states the same conclusion. The Donatist error is not a museum piece. It reappears whenever a Catholic says that a priest's sins invalidate his Mass, or that a baptism by a schismatic community cannot be real, or that a sacrament received from a priest later convicted of abuse must be repeated. Each of those claims locates the sacrament's efficacy in the minister's standing, and each is refuted by the same argument. The contrast with 2020 is instructive: there the defect was in the sign, and no amount of good intention could repair it; here the defect is in the minister's soul, and no amount of personal wickedness can damage the sign. Two different elements, two different errors, one principle: the sacrament is Christ's act, performed through a sign he instituted, and both the sign and the act have to be what he gave.
depth.mistake: The Donatist error is the first and oldest: the sacrament's validity depends on the minister's holiness or orthodoxy, so that a sinful priest's sacraments are doubtful and a separated community's baptism must be repeated. Its diagnostic is that it cannot explain why the Church has always accepted baptism from heretics and sinners, and it usually coexists with a morbid preoccupation with the personal qualities of clergy, which is a pastoral problem as much as a doctrinal one. The second error is the opposite and more modern: an indifference to the sign, in which any sincere intention and any words that seem to express the right idea are treated as sufficient, on the assumption that God is not bound by formulas. Its diagnostic is that it cannot explain why the Church would ever refuse to accept a baptism, and it makes the 2020 response unintelligible. The third error is the communal one, prevalent in liturgical theology: treating the assembly as the minister of the sacrament, so that 'we baptise' seems an improvement because it is more inclusive. The 2020 note addresses exactly this, and its answer is not a defence of clericalism but a statement about who acts: Christ acts in his Church through a minister, and the assembly is the recipient and the co-celebrant of the worship, not the subject of the sacramental act. All three errors confuse the levels at which the Church's faith, the minister's intention and the sign's elements operate.
depth.application: Task (nonblocking, 50 minutes): construct a one-page validity checklist for baptism with five lines, one for matter, form, minister, intention and subject, each with the text that grounds it and one example of a defect. Then apply it to three cases: the emergency baptism by the nurse; a baptism performed by an Orthodox priest with the correct formula; and a baptism performed in a community that uses 'Creator, Redeemer, Sustainer' for the three persons. For each case, state whether the sacrament exists, whether it may be repeated, and what the pastoral consequence is. Model line: 'Intention: the minister must intend at least to do what the Church does, which Trent Session 7 canon 11 protects by anathematising its denial; a defect would be a performance understood by the minister as a purely social gesture; consequence, no sacrament.' Rubric: the intention line must distinguish the minimal intention Trent requires from the faith the minister may lack; the subject line must explain the character; and the third case must be answered by reasoning from the elements rather than by an appeal to the community's sincerity. A checklist that lists only words and water has missed half the sacrament.
depth.summary: A sacrament exists when the sign Christ instituted is performed: suitable matter, determinate form, a minister with the required power, the intention at least of doing what the Church does, and a capable subject. Trent defined the efficacy ex opere operato and required the minister's intention while denying that his worth confers or destroys the sacrament, and the Church distinguishes validity from liceity and from fruitfulness. The 2020 response on the formula 'We baptise you' applied the doctrine: the form was defective, the baptism invalid, and those concerned must be baptised absolutely, since the minister's good intention cannot supply for an altered sign. The Donatist error, which locates the sacrament in the minister's holiness, and the modern error, which locates it in the community's sincerity, are mirror images; both are answered by the principle that Christ acts through the sign he gave, in the person of the minister who performs it.

readings.title: Council of Trent, Session 7 (1547), canons on the sacraments in general, in the Waterworth translation
readings.note: Read canons 1 to 13. The ones the lesson uses are canon 8 on grace conferred ex opere operato, canon 11 on the minister's intention, and canon 12 on the minister in mortal sin, which is the answer to the Donatists in conciliar form. Note the shape of the canons: each anathematises a specific proposition, which is why they are useful for teaching the difference between a defined point and its later elaboration. Public-domain translation on an academic site, not the Holy See edition.

readings.title: Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, response and doctrinal note on the validity of baptism conferred with a modified formula (24 June 2020)
readings.note: Read the two questions and answers first, then the note. The sentences to mark are those on the faith of the Church expressed 'not only by the minister's intention but also by the formula and matter', and on the minister acting 'in the person of Christ who acts in his Church'. The practical answers, that such baptism is invalid and that the persons must be baptised in forma absoluta, are the ones a parish needs. Holy See edition.

Note the Catechism's statement that the ordinary ministers are the bishop, priest and deacon, and that in case of necessity anyone with the right intention may baptise, which is the basis for the nurse example. visual.title: Five elements, three judgments
visual.description: A pentagon of the constitutive elements of a sacrament, with each vertex carrying a defect example, and a side key separating validity, liceity and fruitfulness.
steps: Centre label THE SACRAMENTAL SIGN, with five vertices around it: MATTER (water, oil, bread and wine), FORM (the determinate words), MINISTER (the power required), INTENTION (at least to do what the Church does), SUBJECT (capable of receiving, and not already bearing the character).

Outside each vertex, a defect card: sand instead of water; 'We baptise you'; a layperson absolving; a social gesture without intention; a person already baptised. Each card is stamped with the consequence, 'no sacrament', except the subject card, which reads 'cannot be repeated'.

A side key in three columns: VALIDITY (does the sign exist, per the five elements), LICEITY (was it lawful, citing the case of a valid baptism by an excommunicated minister), FRUITFULNESS (what grace the recipient receives, depending on disposition).

Below the pentagon, the Donatist arrow drawn and crossed out: 'the minister's sin empties the sign', with Trent Session 7 canon 12 cited at the crossing point and a note that the arrow must point at the elements, not at the minister's soul.

A footer timeline with two marks: 1547 Trent Session 7, which defines the elements in controversy, and 2020, when the congregation applies them to an altered formula and requires baptism in forma absoluta.

lessons.title: Liturgical discipline as a test case: Summorum Pontificum, Traditionis Custodes, and reading a motu proprio
lessons.explanation: This lesson is the level's capstone because it takes the distinction that has run through every unit, between what is defined, what is authoritative and what is disciplinary, and applies it to the most contested liturgical question of the last two decades. The doctrinal floor is firm and must be stated first. The Council of Trent defined in Session 22 that the Mass is a true and proper sacrifice offered to God for the living and the dead, in Session 13 that the body and blood of Christ are truly present, and in Session 23 that the priesthood is a sacrament instituted by Christ; the Second Vatican Council's Sacrosanctum Concilium calls the liturgy the summit toward which the Church's activity is directed (SC 10) and states in SC 22 that 'the regulation of the sacred liturgy depends solely on the authority of the Church, that is, on the Apostolic See and, as laws may determine, on the bishop', adding that no one, not even a priest, may add, remove or change anything on his own authority. Nothing in the documents considered here touches any of that. What they touch is law: which books may be used, by whom, where, and with whose permission. The 1962 typical edition of the Roman Missal was promulgated by John XXIII; the Missal of Paul VI was promulgated in 1969 and issued in a typical edition in 1970. In 2007 Benedict XVI issued Summorum Pontificum, whose first article permits the celebration of the Mass according to the 1962 edition 'and never abrogated, as an extraordinary form of the Liturgy of the Church', and his letter to the bishops explained the intention: 'there is no contradiction between the two editions of the Roman Missal', and the two are 'two Forms of one and the same Rite'. In 2021 Francis issued Traditionis Custodes, whose first article states instead that the liturgical books promulgated by Paul VI and John Paul II 'are the unique expression of the lex orandi of the Roman Rite'. The articles that matter for practice are these. Article 2 makes the diocesan bishop, as moderator of the liturgical life of his church, the one whose exclusive competence it is to authorise the use of the 1962 Missal. Article 3 governs existing groups: the bishop is to establish that they do not deny the validity and legitimacy of the liturgical reform, to designate one or more locations for their celebrations, expressly 'not however in the parochial churches and without the erection of new personal parishes', to fix the days and require the readings in the vernacular, to appoint a priest as his delegate, to review the personal parishes already erected, and not to authorise new groups. Article 4 provides that a priest ordained after the publication of the motu proprio who wishes to use the 1962 Missal must make a formal request, and the bishop 'shall consult the Apostolic See before granting this authorization'. Article 5 requires priests who already celebrate according to the 1962 Missal to request authorisation to continue. Article 8 abrogates 'previous norms, instructions, permissions, and customs that do not conform' to the new provisions. The congregation's responses of 4 December 2021 then answered the practical questions: the bishop cannot himself open a parish church, but the congregation may, at his request, permit one only where it is established that no other church, oratory or chapel can be used, and then not at the parish's scheduled Mass times; the older Ritual may be permitted only for personal parishes already canonically erected that use the 1962 Missal, and the older Pontifical is not permitted at all. Three levels follow, and the lesson's whole purpose is to keep them apart. Doctrine: the sacrificial character of the Mass, the real presence, the ministerial priesthood, the validity of both missals. Discipline: permissions, places, numbers, the legal standing of groups, all of which the Apostolic See may grant and withdraw. Juridical and theological opinion: whether the 1962 Missal had ever been abrogated before 2007, whether article 1 of Traditionis Custodes is a doctrinal statement or a legal norm, and whether a faculty granted in 2007 created a right that a later pope could not revoke.
lessons.example: Take a parish that wants a weekly Mass in the older rite and work the canonical path, because the exercise shows how much of the dispute is about procedure. Step one: identify the group. Article 3 applies to groups that already celebrate according to the pre-reform missal, and its first requirement is that the bishop determine that they do not deny the validity and legitimacy of the liturgical reform; a group that treats the reformed Mass as invalid has disqualified itself by its own position, not by the bishop's preference. Step two: the place. Article 3 section 2 excludes parochial churches and forbids the erection of new personal parishes, so the ordinary route is a designated church, oratory or chapel that is not parochial; if none can be found, the bishop may ask the congregation for a parish church, and the responses allow it only on a finding of impossibility, outside the parish's scheduled Masses, and subject to withdrawal when another venue becomes available. Step three: the priest. If he was ordained after 16 July 2021, article 4 requires a formal request and the bishop must consult the Apostolic See before granting it; if he was ordained earlier and already celebrates in the older rite, article 5 requires him to ask for authorisation to continue. Step four: the manner. The readings are to be in the vernacular, using translations approved for liturgical use, and the celebrant uses the 1962 Missal but not the older Pontifical, while the older Ritual is available only in the narrow case the responses describe. Now notice what the path does not require. It does not require anyone to say that the older rite was doctrinally defective, and it does not permit anyone to say that the newer missal is invalid; it requires obedience to the law in force and honesty about what the law is. A parish that follows the path and is refused has a grievance it can pursue through the bishop and the Holy See; a parish that ignores the path has a political gesture, and the gesture will be used by both sides as evidence that the other is acting in bad faith.
lessons.question: A parishioner asks whether the older Mass has been 'banned', and adds that she has read that Pope Benedict said it was never abrogated, so a later pope cannot have forbidden it. What is the accurate answer?
lessons.answer: The accurate answer distinguishes three things. First, the older Mass is not banned in the sense of being declared invalid or illicit in itself: the 1962 Missal was approved by the Apostolic See, its canon is Catholic, and no document has said that celebrating according to it is inherently sinful. Second, its public use is now regulated much more tightly: Traditionis Custodes makes the bishop the moderator of liturgical life and gives him exclusive competence to authorise the 1962 Missal (article 2), excludes parochial churches and new personal parishes (article 3 section 2), requires a formal request and consultation of the Apostolic See for priests ordained after the motu proprio (article 4), requires priests already celebrating to seek authorisation to continue (article 5), and abrogates non-conforming norms, permissions and customs (article 8). Third, Benedict's phrase 'never abrogated' was a juridical statement about the 1962 typical edition, made in the exercise of the same authority that Francis later used to replace the norms; a pope's disciplinary act can be revised by a later pope, and the phrase was contested among canonists even in 2007. So the parishioner is right that the rite is not condemned and wrong that a later pope cannot restrict its use, and the word 'banned' is doing the work of obscuring both points.
lessons.distractor: The older Mass has been banned: a later pope cannot contradict an earlier one, so the only way to make sense of Traditionis Custodes is that the Church has now judged the 1962 Missal to be doctrinally defective, which is why its use is restricted and why Benedict's letter is no longer cited.
lessons.correction: The distractor starts from a false premise about papal authority and arrives at a conclusion no document supports. A pope is not bound by his predecessor's disciplinary acts: the same authority that granted the faculty can withdraw it, which is why article 8 can abrogate permissions that do not conform without any claim that the earlier pope erred in doctrine, and why the Church's legal history is full of norms replaced by later norms. From that false premise the distractor infers a doctrinal judgment from a legal restriction, which is the characteristic error of the whole lesson: if restriction implied defect, the Church's own successive missals would condemn one another. And the distractor's final clause is simply untrue as a matter of fact: Benedict's letter remains an ecclesial document of the first rank, cited by canonists on all sides, and its theological argument about the continuity of the Roman rite is not withdrawn by a change in permissions. The correct answer, by contrast, can name the doctrine that both missals presuppose and the law that currently governs their use, and it can hold them without embarrassment.

depth.definitions: Motu proprio: a legislative act of the pope issued on his own initiative, the instrument used for both Summorum Pontificum (2007) and Traditionis Custodes (2021). Typical edition: the normative Latin text of a liturgical book, of which the 1962 and 1970 missals are the relevant examples. Extraordinary form: Benedict XVI's term for the use of the 1962 Missal under the 2007 norms, now superseded. Lex orandi: the Church's pattern of prayer, which Traditionis Custodes article 1 invokes in calling the post-conciliar books its unique expression. Abrogation: the repeal of a law or permission, effected for non-conforming norms by article 8. Dispensation: the relaxation of a law in a particular case, which in the case of parish churches the congregation may grant at the bishop's request and the bishop may not grant himself. Prerequisites: liturgical reform (43), the sacrificial character of the Mass (44), and the doctrine and discipline distinction (78, 88).
depth.mechanism: How can two popes describe the same liturgical books in incompatible-sounding terms without either being wrong about the faith? Because each is doing a different kind of act. Benedict's letter makes a theological and historical argument: the Roman rite has a continuous history, the 1962 Missal and the 1970 Missal are two expressions of one tradition, and the older one was never formally suppressed, so its use need not be feared as a rejection of the Council. Francis's article 1 makes a juridical determination about which books are normative for the Roman rite now, using the language of the lex orandi to say that the post-conciliar books are the Church's prayer in this rite. The two claims are not contradictories if the first is read as a statement about continuity of tradition and the second as a statement about legal normativity, and that reading is available because the documents themselves are of different genres. What makes the dispute bitter is that both sides use doctrinal-sounding language for juridical claims: 'never abrogated' sounds like a doctrine of indefectibility, and 'unique expression of the lex orandi' sounds like a judgment about the other books. The mechanism the student needs is genre recognition: identify the act, its object, and its addressee before deciding what it claims, which is the skill lesson 34 taught and this lesson tests under pressure.
depth.secondExample: Take the objection that the two papal characterisations cannot both be true, and work it as a case in the interpretation of acts. Benedict wrote that the two missals are 'two Forms of one and the same Rite'. Francis wrote that the post-conciliar books are 'the unique expression of the lex orandi of the Roman Rite'. A reader who treats both sentences as doctrinal propositions about the nature of the liturgy has a contradiction. A reader who asks what each act was doing has none: Benedict was granting a faculty and justifying it by an argument about continuity, so his sentence explains why the older use is not a rupture; Francis was reorganising the law and needed to say which books govern the Roman rite, so his sentence identifies the normative books. The second sentence does not deny that the older books were once the Church's prayer, and the first does not deny that the newer books are now normative. Two further points complete the analysis. First, the fact that a later act narrows an earlier permission is not evidence that the earlier act was dishonest; it is what legislative succession looks like, and the Church's liturgical history contains many such successions, including the replacement of the 1962 missal itself. Second, no Catholic is bound to hold either that the older rite is doctrinally defective or that the newer rite is invalid, and a person who asserts either has moved from a juridical dispute to a doctrinal claim that the magisterium has not made.
depth.mistake: The traditionalist error treats a disciplinary permission as a right and a doctrinal possession, so that any restriction is read as an attack on the faith and the earlier pope's language is treated as a constitutional guarantee. Its diagnostic is that it cannot name the doctrine that Traditionis Custodes denies, and it usually ends by impugning the good faith of the legislator. The progressive error treats the restriction as a doctrinal verdict, so that affection for the older rite becomes evidence of dissent from the Council; its diagnostic is that it cannot explain why the Church continues to recognise the validity of the 1962 Missal and why Benedict's theological argument was never answered, only superseded in law. A third error belongs to journalists and to some canonists: reporting the conflict as a personal rivalry between pontificates, which obscures the fact that both acts are exercises of the same authority and that the later one governs. The common root of all three is the failure to ask what kind of act is in front of one, which is why this lesson closes the unit: the same failure produced the errors about indulgences, about the grades of assent and about the synod. The discipline is not neutrality, since a Catholic owes obedience to the law in force and may have strong views about the wisdom of either act; the discipline is to state the law accurately, to name the doctrine that is not in question, and to keep one's prudential preferences in the register where they belong.
depth.application: Task (nonblocking, 60 minutes): take the text of Traditionis Custodes articles 1 to 5 and 8 and produce a three-column analysis in which every operative sentence is classified as DOCTRINE, DISCIPLINE or JURIDICAL OPINION, with a note on what would count as evidence for the classification. Then write two short texts. The first is a 120-word answer to a parishioner who asks 'was the old Mass banned?', which must use the words valid, regulated and abrogated correctly. The second is a 120-word note to a pastor explaining the canonical steps for a stable group that wants the older rite, citing the articles and the 2021 responses. Rubric: the first text may not use the word 'banned' without quotation marks and an explanation; the second must name the bishop's role under article 2, the restriction on parochial churches in article 3 section 2, the consultation of the Holy See in article 4, and the narrow permission the congregation may grant; and no text may describe either missal as doctrinally defective or invalid. A submission that treats article 1 as a definition has failed, and so has one that treats article 8 as a doctrinal judgment on the 1962 Missal.
depth.summary: The liturgical question of the last two decades is a test of the doctrine and discipline distinction. The doctrinal floor is Trent's teaching on the sacrifice of the Mass, the real presence and the ministerial priesthood, together with Sacrosanctum Concilium 22 on the Church's authority over the liturgy; neither missal is in question as to validity. Summorum Pontificum (2007) permitted the 1962 Missal as an extraordinary form and called it never abrogated; Traditionis Custodes (2021) made the post-conciliar books the unique expression of the Roman rite's lex orandi, gave the bishop exclusive competence to authorise the older Missal, excluded parochial churches and new personal parishes, required consultation of the Apostolic See for priests ordained after the motu proprio, and abrogated non-conforming permissions, with the 2021 responses limiting what a bishop may do on his own. These are legislative acts that a later pope may replace, not doctrinal verdicts, and the characteristic errors are reading a restriction as a judgment of defect and reading a permission as an irrevocable right.

readings.title: Pope Benedict XVI, Summorum Pontificum (7 July 2007), articles 1-12
readings.note: Read article 1 for the two phrases the lesson analyses, 'never abrogated' and 'extraordinary form', and read articles 2 to 7 for the faculties granted, since the contrast with the 2021 act is the substance of the lesson. Note the genre: a motu proprio granting faculties, not a doctrinal constitution. Holy See edition.

readings.title: Pope Benedict XVI, letter to the bishops accompanying Summorum Pontificum (7 July 2007)
readings.note: Read the letter for the argument the motu proprio presupposes: 'there is no contradiction between the two editions of the Roman Missal', the two Forms of one Rite, and the Pope's account of the fears he was answering. This is the text to cite when someone claims that the older rite was doctrinally suspect, and it is also the text that shows how much of the 2007 settlement rested on a theological argument rather than on law alone.

readings.title: Pope Francis, Traditionis Custodes (16 July 2021), articles 1-8, with the accompanying letter to the bishops
readings.note: Read all eight articles, then the letter. Mark article 1 (unique expression of the lex orandi), article 2 (the bishop's exclusive competence), article 3 (existing groups, with section 2 excluding parochial churches and new personal parishes), article 4 (priests ordained after the motu proprio, with consultation of the Apostolic See), article 5 (priests already celebrating) and article 8 (abrogation of non-conforming norms). Note that the numbering is not the numbering used in most commentary, so quote article and section together.

readings.title: Congregation for Divine Worship and the Discipline of the Sacraments, responses to questions on Traditionis Custodes (4 December 2021)
readings.note: Read the responses for the points that decide the parish case: a parish church may be permitted by the congregation, at the bishop's request, only where it is impossible to use another church, oratory or chapel, and not at the parish's scheduled Masses; the older Ritual may be permitted only for personal parishes already canonically erected that use the 1962 Missal; the older Pontifical is not permitted. These responses turn general norms into procedure, and they show that the discipline is more restrictive than the motu proprio's bare articles suggest. Holy See edition.
