questions.prompt: During a parliamentary debate on abolishing the death penalty, one Catholic legislator says the Catechism's word 'inadmissible' is only a policy preference that legislators may disregard, while another says the 1992 edition of the Catechism, which allowed recourse to the penalty in principle, taught something the Church has now admitted was wrong. Using the 2018 letter of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith and Evangelium Vitae 56, assess both.
questions.answer: Both flatten a layered change. The 2018 letter says the revised text of 2267 'situates itself in continuity with the preceding Magisterium while bringing forth a coherent development of Catholic doctrine', and that the new formulation 'expresses an authentic development of doctrine that is not in contradiction with the prior teachings of the Magisterium'. It explains the earlier teaching as belonging to 'a social context in which the penal sanctions were understood differently, and had developed in an environment in which it was more difficult to guarantee that the criminal could not repeat his crime'. On that account the constant is the state's duty to protect the innocent and the inviolability of the person; the change is the judgment that, given modern detention, the penalty is no longer necessary and attacks a dignity that is not lost by crime. John Paul II had already moved the argument in Evangelium Vitae 56, where the cases in which execution is 'an absolute necessity' are said to be 'very rare, if not practically non-existent'. A legislator may therefore argue about means and timetable, but not treat the teaching as a preference; and a Catholic may not say the earlier Catechism was heretical, because the same magisterium has said it was not.
questions.distractor: The first legislator is right in substance: because the change was made on prudential grounds about detention conditions, 'inadmissible' expresses a policy judgment, and a Catholic legislator who judges that abolition would endanger the public may vote to retain the penalty. The second legislator is also right in principle, since a Catechism that once permitted what is now called an attack on human dignity cannot have been teaching the truth.
questions.correction: The distractor splits the two halves of the 2018 letter and then draws a conclusion from each that the letter forbids. It is true that the change turns partly on circumstances, and the letter says so; it does not follow that the resulting teaching is a policy preference, because the letter calls it 'an authentic development of doctrine' and locates the constant in the dignity of the person, which is a moral principle rather than a forecast. It is also true that the earlier text permitted recourse; it does not follow that the earlier text was heretical, since the letter's account is that a principle was applied to circumstances that have changed, and the Church's own reading of its past is that this is continuity, not reversal. The correct position holds three things together: the constant principle, the developed judgment that the penalty is now inadmissible, and the genuine but limited room for prudential argument about how abolition is to be achieved.

questions.prompt: A teacher tells a class that because the Church tolerated slavery for centuries and now teaches that it is intrinsically evil, doctrine is simply the reflection of social consensus; a student replies that the Church always condemned slavery in principle, so nothing changed at all. Using Gaudium et Spes 27, Veritatis Splendor 80 and the 1839 letter In Supremo Apostolatus, give the accurate account.
questions.answer: Neither account survives the documents. The Church did not merely tolerate slavery as a private practice: papal acts of the fifteenth century granted rights over non-Christian peoples that were later invoked to justify the Atlantic trade, theologians defended servitude with arguments from Aristotle and from the law of nations, and an 1866 reply of the Holy Office, approved by Pius IX, held that slavery considered in itself was not contrary to natural law while urging restraint in the trade. Against that, Gregory XVI's In Supremo Apostolatus (1839) condemned the traffic, Paul III had condemned the enslavement of the Indians in Sublimis Deus (1537), and the modern magisterium states the opposite of the 1866 reply: Gaudium et Spes 27 lists 'slavery, prostitution, the selling of women and children' among the infamies that dishonour the Creator, and Veritatis Splendor 80 cites that list as examples of acts which are 'always seriously wrong by reason of their object'. So the change is real, it concerns the moral evaluation of an institution and not merely its circumstances, and it is not a case of doctrine following fashion, because the principle that generated the change, the dignity of the person as image of God, was taught throughout.
questions.distractor: The teacher is right that the change tracks social consensus, since the Church abandoned slavery only after the abolitionist movements had won; the student is right that no doctrinal change occurred, because the Church's condemnation of the slave trade in 1839 already contained everything that Gaudium et Spes later said, and the intervening theological defences of servitude were the opinions of individual writers with no magisterial weight.
questions.correction: The distractor rescues the student's conclusion by suppressing the evidence that makes the case hard, and it credits the teacher's conclusion with a causal story the documents do not support. The 1866 reply is not the opinion of an individual writer; it was an act of a Roman congregation approved by the pope, and it stated in the abstract what the modern magisterium denies. In Supremo Apostolatus condemned the trade, not the institution as such, and said nothing about the moral status of slaveholding in a society where it was legal. So the honest account is neither that nothing changed nor that everything is fashion: an unchanged principle of human dignity, held from the beginning but applied unevenly and sometimes contradicted by the Church's own acts, eventually generated a judgment that the institution itself is intrinsically evil, and that judgment required the Church to recognise that earlier defences were wrong. That recognition is what the modern documents presuppose and what makes the case the hardest test of any theory of development.

questions.prompt: A parish bulletin announces: 'Plenary indulgence for the faithful departed: enrol your deceased relatives for a donation of twenty pounds; all temporal punishment and the guilt of sin are remitted.' A parishioner asks whether this is what the Church teaches. Using the Council of Trent's decree on indulgences, the Catechism 1471-1479 and Paul VI's Indulgentiarum Doctrina, identify each error in the announcement.
questions.answer: Four errors, of different kinds. First, the announcement says the guilt of sin is remitted; Trent's doctrine and the Catechism's definition both say an indulgence remits 'the temporal punishment due to sins whose guilt has already been forgiven' (CCC 1471), so guilt is the business of the sacrament of penance, not of an indulgence. Second, it attaches a donation as the price of the grant; Trent ordered that 'all base and illicit bargains' connected with indulgences be wholly abolished, and the offering attached to an indulgence must be a free almsgiving, not a fee. Third, it promises a plenary indulgence for the dead as though the Church could absolve them; the Church's act regarding the dead is suffrage, a prayer of intercession, not a juridical sentence, and the Catechism's phrasing is that the faithful 'can gain indulgences for themselves or apply them to the dead' (CCC 1471). Fourth, it omits the conditions: for a plenary indulgence the norms require confession, communion, prayer for the pope's intentions and the absence of all attachment to sin, including venial sin (Indulgentiarum Doctrina, norm 7). What is sound in the announcement is the doctrine itself: that the Church has power from Christ to remit temporal punishment by applying the treasury of the satisfactions of Christ and the saints.
questions.distractor: The announcement is substantially correct: Trent defended the practice of indulgences against Luther, so the Church does claim power over the punishment and guilt of sin, and the offering is legitimate because indulgences have always been attached to almsgiving and to the building of churches, which is why the 1517 indulgence was lawful in itself.
questions.correction: The distractor repeats the confusion the Reformation was about and then compounds it with a historical error. Trent's decree defines the power to grant indulgences and calls their use 'most salutary', but the same decree orders abuses corrected, and the Council's doctrine distinguishes the temporal punishment that remains after guilt is forgiven, a distinction the Catechism states in the definition at 1471. On the offering, the distractor concedes too much: almsgiving can be one of the works to which an indulgence is attached, but Trent's abolition of 'base and illicit bargains' and the 1967 reform's removal of the older arithmetic of days and years were both aimed at the impression that a grant can be bought or measured. On 1517, the distractor's history is wrong in the relevant respect: the question was never whether almsgiving could accompany an indulgence, but whether the grant was being preached in a way that made forgiveness seem purchasable, which is what Luther's ninety-five theses attacked and what Trent then legislated against.

questions.prompt: A diocese discovers that for fifteen years baptisms in one parish were conferred with the formula 'We baptise you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit'. Using the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith's 2020 response and the canons of the Council of Trent on the sacraments, state what has happened, what must now be done, and why the minister's good intention did not save the rite.
questions.answer: On the 2020 response, such baptisms are invalid, and those so baptised 'must be baptised in forma absoluta', that is, unconditionally rather than conditionally, because no baptism occurred. The doctrinal note explains why: the faith of the Church is expressed in the sacramental act 'not only by the minister's intention but also by the formula and matter', and the change from 'I' to 'We' alters the formula in a way that obscures who is acting. The minister does not baptise in his own name but 'in the person of Christ who acts in his Church', and the first person singular is the linguistic form of that acting; a congregational 'we' makes the community the subject of the rite. The intention was presumably good, and the Trent canons on intention (Session 7, canon 11) require only that the minister intend at least to do what the Church does, but an intention cannot supply for a defective form, because the sacrament is constituted by sign as well as by intention. Practically: the records must be annotated, the persons baptised absolutely with the correct formula, and the confirmations and ordinations that depended on the invalid baptism examined, since orders and confirmation presuppose baptism.
questions.distractor: The baptisms are valid but illicit: the minister's intention to do what the Church does was present, the water and the Trinitarian names were used, and Trent's canon on intention (Session 7, canon 11) is satisfied, so the diocese should record the defect and regularise the liturgy without rebaptising anyone, since rebaptism is forbidden.
questions.correction: The distractor knows two true things and misapplies both. It is true that Trent requires only a minimal intention, and true that rebaptism is forbidden; but the prohibition of rebaptism presupposes that a baptism has taken place, and the 2020 response's whole point is that where the form is substantially altered there is no baptism to repeat. The distractor also invokes the intention in the wrong place: the intention is one element of the sign, and the Church's judgment is that the words are another element, so a right intention joined to a wrong form produces no sacrament, just as a right form joined to no intention produces none. The 'valid but illicit' category is real and important, and this is precisely not a case of it: validity concerns whether the sacrament exists, liceity concerns whether its celebration was lawful, and the 2020 note locates the defect in the first.

questions.prompt: Two Catholics argue about the 2021 motu proprio Traditionis Custodes. The first says it abrogated the traditional Latin Mass, proving that the 1962 Missal had been doctrinally defective all along. The second says no pope can restrict the older rite, because the Mass of Pius V was established by the Church's immutable tradition and a pope has no authority over it. Using Sacrosanctum Concilium 22, Summorum Pontificum article 1 and Traditionis Custodes article 1, adjudicate.
questions.answer: Both claims mistake the level at which the documents operate. Sacrosanctum Concilium 22 states that 'the regulation of the sacred liturgy depends solely on the authority of the Church', exercised by the Apostolic See and, within limits, by the bishop; so liturgical permissions are disciplinary acts that a pope may grant, narrow or withdraw, and both motu proprio are such acts. Summorum Pontificum article 1 called the 1962 Missal a form 'never abrogated' and permitted its use as an extraordinary form; Traditionis Custodes article 1 states instead that the books promulgated by Paul VI and John Paul II 'are the unique expression of the lex orandi of the Roman Rite', and article 8 abrogates the previous norms, instructions, permissions and customs that do not conform to it. That is a reversal of discipline, not of doctrine: neither document touches the canon of the Mass, the doctrine of eucharistic sacrifice (Trent, Session 22) or the validity of either missal, and both missals were approved by the Apostolic See. What remains open is a juridical question canonists argue: whether the 1962 Missal was ever abrogated, and whether a permission withdrawn leaves a rite forbidden or merely unregulated.
questions.distractor: The first Catholic is right about the effect and roughly right about the reason: the Church would not withdraw a rite it considered orthodox, so the restrictions confirm that the older missal carried defective doctrine about the sacrifice and the priesthood. The second is right about principle but wrong about this pope, since a general council alone could reverse the traditional Mass.
questions.correction: The distractor infers doctrine from discipline, which is the error both the lesson and the documents are designed to prevent, and it adds a false claim about councils. If withdrawal of a permission implied doctrinal defect, the same inference would condemn the 1962 missal's own predecessors, which the Church also replaced, and would make liturgical reform impossible in principle; Sacrosanctum Concilium 22 locates authority over the liturgy in the Church precisely because rites are not doctrines. The claim that only a council could act is also wrong: Paul VI's 1969 missal and John XXIII's 1962 edition were both acts of the Apostolic See, and the motu proprio is the ordinary instrument by which popes legislate in this area. What the distractor cannot do is say which doctrinal proposition either missal denies, and that inability is the tell: a claim about doctrine that cannot name the doctrine is a claim about taste.

questions.prompt: A study day asks participants to sort four claims into 'defined', 'authoritative but not defined' and 'legitimate theological opinion'. The claims are: (1) the one Church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church; (2) a definition of the Roman Pontiff is irreformable of itself and not by the consent of the Church; (3) the 1962 Missal was never juridically abrogated; (4) the precise theological note by which the reservation of ordination to men is taught. Which sorting is correct, and why?
questions.answer: Defined: (2), which is the fourth chapter of Pastor Aeternus, promulgated in 1870, and is a dogma in the strict sense. Authoritative but not defined: (1) and (3). The 'subsists in' clause belongs to the doctrinal constitution Lumen Gentium 8, whose teaching the 2007 responses of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith treat as binding and not negotiable, but Vatican II deliberately issued no new dogmatic definitions, and the clause's function is to state the identity of the one Church of Christ with the Catholic Church rather than to add an article to the creed. Claim (3) is a juridical statement about the 1962 typical edition, made in Summorum Pontificum article 1 and reversed in its legal effect by Traditionis Custodes, which shows that it was discipline and not doctrine. Legitimate theological opinion: (4), the question whether the teaching belongs to the first or the second paragraph of the Profession of Faith, which the 1995 response and the commentary on Ad Tuendam Fidem answer differently and which theologians argue without denying the obligation to hold the teaching.
questions.distractor: Defined: (1), (2) and (4), since all three concern faith and morals and the Church has spoken on all of them; authoritative but not defined: (3), because a missal is a legal book; legitimate opinion: nothing, because once the magisterium has addressed a question there is no room for theological opinion, only for assent or dissent.
questions.correction: The distractor uses 'the Church has spoken on it' as a single category, which is the error the exercise exists to catch. That a question concerns faith and morals does not make the answer a definition; Lumen Gentium's teaching on the Church, the 2007 responses and the two motu proprio all concern faith, morals or worship, and they carry different weights. It also misplaces (4): the classification of a teaching within the paragraphs of the Profession of Faith is exactly the kind of question on which the magisterium has left work to theology, and the 1998 commentary itself supplies examples and arguments rather than a definition. Finally, the distractor's last clause erases the third grade altogether, which canon 752 and Ad Tuendam Fidem establish: authentic non-definitive teaching asks for religious submission, and submission is not the same as the assent of faith, nor is disagreement with a theological classification the same as dissent from the teaching.

questions.prompt: A Catholic magistrate in a state that retains capital punishment must sentence a convicted murderer. She accepts the Catechism's statement that the death penalty is inadmissible but argues that in this case the prisons are unsafe and the convict has already killed a guard. Using Catechism 2265-2267 and the 2018 letter of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, what may she conclude, and what may she not conclude?
questions.answer: She may conclude that the state's duty to protect innocent life remains, because the 2018 letter expressly says that 'it remains the duty of public authorities to defend the life of citizens, as has always been taught by the Magisterium and is confirmed by the Catechism of the Catholic Church in numbers 2265 and 2266'. She may also conclude that a sentence of life imprisonment without parole, or transfer to a secure institution, satisfies that duty, since the letter's argument is that 'modern society possesses more efficient detention systems' and that the penalty is therefore 'unnecessary as protection for the life of innocent people'. What she may not conclude is that a particular emergency reopens the licence of the 1992 text, because the developed teaching states that the penalty 'is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person', a dignity the letter says is not lost even after the most serious crimes. The remaining question is prudential in the narrow sense: which means of secure detention actually exist and can be ordered by the court.
questions.distractor: She may impose the penalty, because Catechism 2267 preserves the traditional teaching that recourse to the death penalty is not excluded when this is the only way of effectively defending human lives, and the 2018 revision changed the wording without changing that condition; the emergency she describes satisfies the condition, and the decision is hers as a matter of prudential judgment.
questions.correction: The distractor quotes the 1992 text as though it were still in force, which is the commonest error in this area, and it mistakes the structure of the 2018 argument. The current 2267 does not contain the 'not excluded... if this is the only possible way' formula; it states that the penalty is inadmissible and that the Church works for its abolition worldwide. The 2018 letter does not deny that public authority must defend citizens, but it holds that the defence is now to be secured by other means, and it grounds the inadmissibility in the dignity of the person rather than in the availability of alternatives. The distractor's appeal to prudence is also misplaced: prudential judgment selects means, it does not reopen a judgment the magisterium has said is required by the dignity of the person, and a magistrate who thinks otherwise is not exercising the virtue but substituting her own assessment of the moral object.

questions.prompt: A parish receives an adult who was baptised as an infant by a Methodist minister, with water and the Trinitarian formula, and who now wishes to be received into full communion. A volunteer says she must be baptised conditionally 'to be safe', and another says she must be baptised absolutely because Protestant baptisms are not real baptisms. What is the correct pastoral and doctrinal judgment?
questions.answer: Neither suggestion is right. The Catholic Church recognises baptism conferred with water and the Trinitarian formula by a minister with the intention of doing what the Church does, and Trent's canons on the sacraments (Session 7, canon 8 on the effect ex opere operato and canon 11 on the minister's intention) locate the sacrament's efficacy in Christ's action rather than in the minister's communion or worth. The 2020 response on the altered formula sharpens rather than loosens this: it held invalid a baptism conferred with 'We baptise you', precisely because the form was changed, and it did not suggest that a correctly administered baptism outside the Catholic Church is doubtful. So the adult is baptised, and to baptise her again, even conditionally, would be to treat a sacrament as doubtful without grounds, which is why the Church's law permits conditional baptism only where a prudent doubt about the facts exists. What she needs is a profession of faith and reception, and what the parish needs is evidence about the original administration, not a precautionary rite.
questions.distractor: Conditional baptism is the safe and therefore correct course, because the Church cannot be certain of the minister's intention in a separated community, and a conditional form supplies whatever was lacking without repeating the sacrament; the second volunteer is wrong only in wanting an absolute form.
questions.correction: The distractor treats uncertainty about intention as a standing reason for conditional baptism, which inverts the discipline and obscures the doctrine. The Church presumes the intention of a minister who uses the Church's form and matter, and Trent's canon 11 asks for no more than the intention of doing what the Church does; if doubt were permanent, every baptism outside the visible communion would be repeatable, and the practice of the Church in receiving converts would be unintelligible. Conditional baptism exists for cases of factual doubt, for example where it is unknown whether water was used, and it is not a device for reassuring the anxious. The distractor also repeats the second volunteer's premise in a softer form, since it treats the separated community's ministry as though it could not confer what the Church's own canons say is conferred by the sign. The correct answer distinguishes the sacrament, which is Christ's act, from the ecclesial community's standing, which is a question about communion and not about validity.

questions.prompt: An ecumenical commission issues a report saying that the disagreements between East and West at Florence in 1439 were 'merely cultural misunderstandings about purgatory and papal authority', and that since the union was never received the doctrinal questions remain open. Using the Florentine decree, Lumen Gentium 25 and Pastor Aeternus, assess the report.
questions.answer: The report is wrong on two counts and right on a third. Wrong: the Florentine decree of union was not a cultural document. It states the Latin doctrine that the Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father and the Son and that the addition to the creed was 'licitly and reasonably' made; it states what is to be believed about the pains of purgatory, the life of the blessed and suffrages for the dead; and it states the plenitude of power given to the Apostolic See. Those are doctrinal propositions, and a council in union with the pope proposed them as such. Wrong also: the non-reception of the union does not reopen the questions, because Lumen Gentium 25 holds that to the Church's definitions 'the assent of the Church can never be wanting', and Pastor Aeternus holds that papal definitions are irreformable 'of themselves, and not by the consent of the church'. Right: the failure of reception is a real historical fact that calls for explanation, and the explanation is not that nothing was taught but that the union was imposed under political pressure, that the Greek delegates acted without the mind of their churches, and that the doctrinal formulas were not received in the East. Those are reasons to reformulate, not to declare the questions open.
questions.distractor: The report is broadly correct: Florence's decrees were acts of a council whose union collapsed, and a teaching that the whole Church has not received cannot be binding, so purgatory and the papacy remain legitimate subjects of disagreement between the Churches until a council settles them afresh.
questions.correction: The distractor restates the report's premise in the language of the lesson on reception and thereby shows why that lesson matters. It assumes that reception is a condition of binding force, which is the position Pastor Aeternus and Lumen Gentium 25 exclude; it also makes the further mistake of treating the collapse of a political union as evidence about the content of a decree, when the decree's content can be read. What the distractor cannot account for is the Church's own subsequent conduct: Florence's teaching on purgatory and on the procession of the Spirit continued to be taught and was restated at Trent and in the Catechism, and the ecumenical dialogues have proceeded by re-reading the formulas, not by declaring them unsettled. The honest report would distinguish three things: the doctrinal content, which stands; the formulation and the circumstances of its imposition, which were defective; and the ecumenical task, which is to find a way of stating the same faith that the East can receive.

questions.prompt: A seminarian preparing a presentation lists four papal acts: the definition of the Immaculate Conception in Ineffabilis Deus (1854); the definition of the Assumption in Munificentissimus Deus (1950); Ordinatio Sacerdotalis (1994); and an apostolic exhortation on the family. He asks which are infallible, and on what basis, using the four conditions of Pastor Aeternus and the grades of Ad Tuendam Fidem.
questions.answer: The two definitions are exercises of the extraordinary magisterium and satisfy the four conditions: each pope speaks as pastor and teacher of all Christians, in virtue of supreme apostolic authority, defines a doctrine of faith or morals, and proposes it to the whole Church to be held. Ineffabilis Deus defines that the doctrine of the Immaculate Conception 'has been divinely revealed' and therefore is to be believed firmly and constantly by all the faithful; Munificentissimus Deus defines that the Assumption 'has been revealed by God' and is to be believed. Ordinatio Sacerdotalis is not an ex cathedra definition, but the 1995 response of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith holds that the teaching has been 'set forth infallibly by the ordinary and universal Magisterium', so it is definitive without being a definition; on Ad Tuendam Fidem it belongs at least to the second paragraph of the Profession of Faith, and its classification as first or second paragraph is a matter of theological argument. The apostolic exhortation belongs to the third grade: authentic teaching that asks for religious submission of intellect and will under canon 752, not the assent of faith.
questions.distractor: All four are infallible, because each is an act of the pope teaching on faith and morals and the promise of assistance attaches to the papal office as such; the differences between them are differences of solemnity, not of authority, which is why a Catholic owes the same assent to an exhortation as to a definition.
questions.correction: The distractor collapses the grades of assent, which is the single most common error in this whole area, and it does so by extending the promise of assistance to the person rather than to the act. Pastor Aeternus attaches infallibility to a specific kind of act, a definitive definition of doctrine by the universal pastor; Ad Tuendam Fidem then distinguishes truths divinely revealed and believed with divine faith, truths definitively proposed and firmly held, and teaching authentically proposed but not definitive and received with religious submission. Those are not differences of solemnity but of the response asked, and a seminarian who tells a congregation that an exhortation requires the assent of faith will not be able to explain why the Church distinguishes the grades at all, or why a theologian may examine the arguments of an exhortation without being a dissenter. The distractor's final clause also inverts the logic: the lesser grade is not a weaker version of the higher one but a different act with its own proper response.

questions.prompt: A school history textbook states that 'the Church sold forgiveness of sins in the late Middle Ages, until Luther protested and Trent quietly abolished the practice'. Using the Council of Trent's decree on indulgences, Paul VI's Indulgentiarum Doctrina and the Catechism 1471-1479, correct the sentence.
questions.answer: Three corrections. First, 'sold forgiveness of sins': an indulgence remits the temporal punishment due to sins whose guilt has already been forgiven (CCC 1471), and forgiveness of guilt is given in the sacrament of penance; the traffic that provoked the Reformation concerned the preaching of a grant attached to almsgiving, and Trent responded by ordering 'all base and illicit bargains' abolished, not by denying the doctrine. Second, 'Trent quietly abolished the practice': Trent taught and commanded that 'the use of Indulgences, most salutary to the Christian people', be retained in the Church, and anathematised those who say they are useless or deny the Church's power to grant them; what Trent abolished was the abuse. Third, 'quietly': the decree is an explicit act of the twenty-fifth session (1563) which also required moderation and charged bishops with correcting abuses. The reform that did change the practice substantially came much later: Paul VI's Indulgentiarum Doctrina (1967) defined the indulgence in the terms the Catechism now uses, abolished the reckoning in days and years for partial indulgences, insisted that no indulgence is gained without conversion, and reduced the number of plenary grants.
questions.distractor: The sentence is substantially accurate: indulgences were a financial device that financed the building of Saint Peter's, Trent suppressed them in response to Luther, and the modern Church retains only a symbol, which is why the 1967 reform abolished the theology of the treasury along with the arithmetic of days and years.
questions.correction: The distractor accepts the textbook's causal story and then adds two errors of its own. On finance: almsgiving was attached to some grants and the arrangements around the 1517 preaching were scandalous, which Trent addressed; but the doctrine's basis is the power of binding and loosing (Matthew 16:19; 18:18; John 20:23) and the communion of saints, not a fundraising mechanism. On 1967: Paul VI did not abolish the treasury, he re-described it, insisting that it 'should certainly not be imagined as the sum total of material goods accumulated in the course of the centuries' but is the infinite value of Christ's expiation and merits, with the prayers and good works of the saints; and he retained the distinction between plenary and partial indulgences. The sentence the textbook should have written is that a doctrine of the Church's power to remit temporal punishment was badly preached, commercially exploited and then reformed, twice: doctrinally at Trent against denial, and practically in 1967 against confusion.

questions.prompt: A textbook asserts that 'the Catholic Church never condemned slavery until the 1960s, and only changed its mind when public opinion made the old position untenable, which shows that its moral teaching is simply the morality of the surrounding society'. Using papal documents from 1537 and 1839, Gaudium et Spes 27, Veritatis Splendor 80 and the 1866 reply of the Holy Office, evaluate the assertion.
questions.answer: The assertion is false in its chronology and evasive in its conclusion. On chronology: Paul III's Sublimis Deus (1537) condemned the enslavement of the Indians and affirmed their capacity for faith; Gregory XVI's In Supremo Apostolatus (1839) condemned the slave trade as inhuman and contrary to the dignity of the human person, and Leo XIII returned to the question in In Plurimis (1888); Gaudium et Spes 27, promulgated in 1965, lists 'slavery, prostitution, the selling of women and children' among the infamies that dishonour the Creator. On the conclusion: the history is genuinely difficult for the Church, because papal acts of the fifteenth century granted rights that were used to justify the Atlantic trade, theologians elaborated defences of servitude, and in 1866 the Holy Office, with papal approval, held that slavery considered in itself was not contrary to natural law. So the Church's record is not one of steady condemnation, and the modern teaching that slavery is intrinsically evil, which Veritatis Splendor 80 states by citing the conciliar list, required a real development and a recognition of past error. That is not the same as following public opinion, since the principle that drove the change, the image of God in every person, is the Church's own.
questions.distractor: The assertion is right: the Church accommodated slavery for centuries, defended it from Scripture and from Aristotle, and abandoned it only when abolition became politically inevitable, which is evidence that its moral teaching tracks social consensus and that the modern condemnation is therefore revisable in turn.
questions.correction: The distractor's account of the past is closer to the evidence than the textbook's, but its inference fails, and the failure is instructive. The fact that the Church's practice lagged and that some of its acts supported slavery shows that the Church can fail in application and even in particular judgments; it does not show that the teaching is constituted by social consensus, because the abolitionist argument the Church eventually adopted was drawn from its own premises about creation, the image of God and the redemption of every person, and those premises were stated long before abolitionism existed. The distractor also ignores the direction of the moral claim: Veritatis Splendor 80 treats slavery as an act 'always seriously wrong by reason of their object', which is a claim about the act and not about the popularity of condemning it. The correct conclusion distinguishes the Church's doctrine, which generates the condemnation, from the Church's historical record, which includes complicity, and refuses to use the second to dissolve the first.

questions.prompt: A national conference of bishops issues a unanimous statement on a contested public question and describes it as 'the teaching of the Church in this country'. A journalist says it is therefore infallible and a Catholic politician who disagrees is a heretic. Another commentator says a bishops' conference has no teaching authority at all. Using Lumen Gentium 25, Christus Dominus and Ad Tuendam Fidem, assess both.
questions.answer: Both overstate. A conference is an assembly of bishops for a territory, and its statements carry the weight of the bishops' authentic teaching office: they are acts of the ordinary magisterium and ask for religious submission of intellect and will under canon 752, as Ad Tuendam Fidem's third paragraph and the Profession of Faith state. They are not, however, infallible by virtue of being unanimous, because the infallibility Lumen Gentium 25 attributes to the body of bishops belongs to the whole college dispersed and united with Peter's successor, not to a fragment of it acting alone, and the same paragraph insists that no individual bishop is endowed with the prerogative of infallibility. Nor is a conference a council: a particular council or a plenary council has its own legislative standing, and a conference's doctrinal statement is not a definition. The politician's disagreement is therefore not heresy, but if the statement is an authentic application of the Church's moral teaching to a public question it is not a matter of indifference either, and the honest question is whether he is rejecting the teaching or disputing a prudential application.
questions.distractor: The journalist is right: a unanimous conference of bishops teaching on faith and morals is the ordinary universal magisterium at work, so the statement is infallible and dissent from it is heresy. The commentator is right about the law but wrong about the practice, since conferences in fact legislate for their territories and their decrees bind as particular law.
questions.correction: The distractor identifies the right category and applies it to the wrong subject. The ordinary and universal magisterium is the college of bishops united with the pope, teaching definitively while dispersed throughout the world, and Lumen Gentium 25 describes it as such; a national conference is a body of some of the bishops of one region, and no aggregation of bishops short of the whole college with its head can claim that note. The distractor also confuses two kinds of act: a conference may issue particular law for its territory, and that law binds as law, but legislative authority in a territory is not the same as infallible doctrinal teaching, and the statement in question is doctrinal. The correct answer preserves both truths that the distractor smashes together: the statement is authoritative teaching that asks for submission, and it is not a definition, so disagreement with its prudential elements is not heresy while rejection of the moral principle it applies would be.

questions.prompt: A priest announces that he will celebrate Mass according to the 1962 Missal in his parish church every Sunday, citing Summorum Pontificum's statement that the older missal was 'never abrogated', and adding that no bishop can restrict a rite that the Church has used for centuries. Using Traditionis Custodes articles 2, 3, 4 and 8 and the 2021 responses, state the canonical position and identify the theological error in his argument.
questions.answer: Canonically: Traditionis Custodes gives the diocesan bishop exclusive competence to authorise the use of the 1962 Missal (article 2), and article 3 section 2 requires that the locations designated for groups that use it are not parochial churches and that no new personal parishes are erected. A priest ordained after the publication of the motu proprio must make a formal request, and the bishop 'shall consult the Apostolic See before granting this authorization' (article 4); a priest ordained earlier who already celebrates in the older rite must request authorisation to continue (article 5); and article 8 abrogates previous norms, instructions, permissions and customs that do not conform. The 2021 responses add that a parish church may be used only if the congregation permits it, at the bishop's request, on a finding that no other church, oratory or chapel is available, and not at the parish's scheduled Masses. So the announcement is unlawful, and the appeal to 'never abrogated' does not answer it, because the phrase described the previous law, which the same authority has now replaced. The theological error is a category mistake: the priest treats a liturgical permission as though it were a doctrine, and then treats a doctrine as though it were beyond the pope's authority. Sacrosanctum Concilium 22 locates the regulation of the liturgy in the Church's authority, while the substance of the sacraments, which no pope may alter, is not at issue here.
questions.distractor: The priest is within his rights, because Summorum Pontificum established that the 1962 Missal was never abrogated and that any priest may celebrate it without the bishop's permission; a later motu proprio cannot remove a right that rests on the Church's tradition, and article 8 therefore exceeds the pope's authority over the liturgy.
questions.correction: The distractor makes three moves, each of which the documents defeat. It treats a permission granted by one pope as a right immune to the next, when article 8 expressly abrogates the earlier norms and no principle of canon law makes a liturgical faculty irrevocable. It treats the phrase 'never abrogated' as a doctrinal statement, when it was a juridical claim about the 1962 typical edition, controverted among canonists at the time and now superseded. And it asserts that a motu proprio can exceed the pope's authority over the liturgy, which contradicts Sacrosanctum Concilium 22 and the practice of every pontificate since Pius V: missals have been promulgated, revised and withdrawn by the Apostolic See for four centuries. The distractor's strongest point, that the older rite is lawful and has never been condemned, is compatible with everything in Traditionis Custodes, which regulates its use rather than denying its validity.

questions.prompt: A theologian publishes an article arguing that a particular teaching, which the Church has proposed as definitive, in fact belongs to the third paragraph of the Profession of Faith and should therefore be open to public dissent. A colleague replies that the classification is settled and the article is simply dissent. Which position is defensible, and what does each of them get wrong?
questions.answer: The first position is defensible only in part and the second is too quick. Defensible: arguing about the correct theological note of a teaching is a legitimate theological task, and Ad Tuendam Fidem's second paragraph exists precisely because there are truths 'definitively proposed' which are not divinely revealed, so the boundary between the second and third paragraphs is a real question that has to be argued from the connection of the teaching to the deposit of faith. Not defensible: the inference that a third-paragraph classification licenses public dissent. Canon 752 requires religious submission of intellect and will to authentic non-definitive teaching, and Ad Tuendam Fidem's third paragraph repeats the formula, so even on the theologian's own classification the teaching would bind, and public dissent would be a failure of that submission rather than a legitimate exercise of theological freedom. The colleague is too quick because classification is not settled by assertion, but the colleague is right that the practical conclusion does not follow from the reclassification, and that is the argument the article actually needs to win.
questions.distractor: The first position is fully defensible, because a teaching that is not divinely revealed cannot be infallible, so any teaching that can be shown to belong to the third paragraph is a matter of opinion and public dissent from it is a service to the Church; the colleague's reply merely restates the magisterium's own preference.
questions.correction: The distractor's first premise is false and its conclusion is a non sequitur. It is false that only divinely revealed teaching can be infallible: the second paragraph of the Profession of Faith covers truths definitively proposed which are not contained in revelation but are required for its faithful exposition, and the Church holds them definitively, as Ad Tuendam Fidem's own account of the matter states. It is a non sequitur because even the third paragraph, which is what the distractor is trying to reach, is not a zone of opinion: canon 752 asks for religious submission of intellect and will, and the refusal of that submission is a different act from the free investigation of arguments. The distractor also mischaracterises the colleague, who need not deny that notes can be argued, only that the argument, even if won, produces the licence claimed. The correct answer distinguishes three things the distractor merges: the truth of a teaching, its theological note, and the response owed to it.

questions.prompt: A diocese declines to implement a Roman instruction on liturgical practice, and a commentator describes this as 'a clear case of non-reception, which in the Church's tradition means the instruction has no force'. Using the lesson on reception, Lumen Gentium 25 and the distinction between doctrine and discipline, evaluate the claim and say what a bishop's refusal does and does not establish.
questions.answer: The claim confuses three senses of reception. Juridically, a Roman instruction is law for the Latin Church and binds once promulgated; a diocese's failure to implement it is a failure of obedience, not a repeal. Theologically, reception is the process by which the whole Church assimilates a teaching in faith, and Lumen Gentium 25's assurance that 'the assent of the Church can never be wanting' to definitions describes a promised effect rather than a condition. Historically, reception names the uneven uptake of councils and reforms, and it can fail: Florence's union collapsed, Lateran V's reform decrees were widely ignored, and the 1967 reform of indulgences took years to reach parishes. What a bishop's refusal establishes is a fact about implementation and, at most, a prudential judgment that the instruction is unworkable in his circumstances, which he must make within the law and may be required to justify. What it does not establish is that the instruction is false or that it has lost force, because force is a juridical property conferred by the legislator and withdrawn by him, not by the governed.
questions.distractor: The claim is correct in substance: reception is the Church's own test of a teaching's validity, so a widely refused instruction has no binding force, and the same principle explains why doctrinal definitions must be received by the faithful before they bind, which is why the Church waits for reception before treating a doctrine as settled.
questions.correction: The distractor makes reception do work the tradition never assigns it and then grounds it in a false premise about definitions. The false premise is the claim that definitions wait for reception before binding; Pastor Aeternus says the opposite in terms, holding that definitions are irreformable 'of themselves, and not by the consent of the church', and Lumen Gentium 25 treats the Church's assent as the promised consequence. The misuse of reception is equally damaging in the other direction: if a refused instruction lost force, every unpopular norm would lapse, and the Church's discipline would be decided by the least compliant diocese. The distractor is right that reception is a real phenomenon with real failures, and the lesson insists on that; but the failures belong to the history of the Church's life, not to the validity of its acts, and the correct answer says which sense of the word is in play before drawing any conclusion.

questions.prompt: A candidate for ordination is asked in examination: 'State what is defined, what is authoritative but not defined, and what is legitimate opinion about the Church, and give one example of each.' His answer begins: 'Defined: that the pope is infallible whenever he teaches; authoritative: that the Church is the Mystical Body of Christ; opinion: whether non-Catholics can be saved.' Assess the answer.
questions.answer: All three items are misplaced. Defined: the creed's four marks, one, holy, catholic and apostolic, and the 1870 definition of papal infallibility, which attaches to a definitive act of the universal pastor defining a doctrine of faith or morals and not to teaching as such; so the candidate's 'whenever he teaches' is precisely the error Pastor Aeternus excludes. Authoritative but not defined: the identification of the one Church of Christ with the Catholic Church in Lumen Gentium 8 and the 2007 responses' reading of 'subsists', which are binding without being definitions; the Mystical Body is scriptural and liturgical language used by Pius XII in Mystici Corporis (1943) and by Lumen Gentium 7, and calling it merely authoritative understates a doctrine that is at least definitively taught. Legitimate opinion: the theological classification of 'subsists in' and the precise relation of the separated communities to the one Church. What is not opinion is whether non-Catholics can be saved: Lumen Gentium 16 and the Church's constant teaching hold that salvation is possible for those who are not formally members, and the candidate has confused a defined necessity, that the Church is the ordinary means of salvation, with an open question about its application.
questions.distractor: The answer is sound in substance: the pope's teaching office is infallible by the promise of Christ, the Mystical Body is a pious image rather than a doctrine, and the salvation of non-Catholics is exactly the kind of question the Church has left open, since the Council declined to say anything definite about it.
questions.correction: The distractor defends each misplacement with a plausible-sounding reason, which is why the exam question exists. On the papacy it repeats the flattening error: infallibility belongs to a kind of act, and Pastor Aeternus's four conditions are the act's description, not a formality. On the Mystical Body it demotes a doctrine to an image: Lumen Gentium 7 teaches that the Church is the Body of Christ and that the members are made one with him, and Pius XII's encyclical of 1943 is an act of the ordinary magisterium treating it as doctrine. On salvation it invents an openness: Lumen Gentium 16 states that those who through no fault of their own do not know Christ may attain eternal life, which is a positive teaching, not a silence. What the distractor reveals is the characteristic shape of the error the pack keeps returning to, which is not getting the grades wrong item by item but lacking the habit of asking what kind of act is in front of one.
